The following issues were deliberated upon during the  
meeting:
1. Immunity
PwC,  namely  PricewaterhouseCoopers  Professional
Services LLP, raised the issue of immunity from civil,
criminal, or administrative claims, liabilities, damages,
and legal proceedings that may arise in connection with the
preparation of the report pursuant to the directions of the
Hon’ble Supreme Court. PwC expressed apprehension that it
might be unnecessarily drawn into frivolous litigation or
proceedings on account of preparing the report in compliance
with the directions of the Hon’ble Court.
Accordingly, PwC requested that the Hon’ble Court
consider passing an appropriate order granting immunity to
PwC and any external specialist or agency engaged by it
from being impleaded, summoned, or otherwise made subject
to,  or  required  to  participate  in,  any  litigation  or
proceeding before any court, tribunal, authority, or other
forum in connection with the services rendered pursuant to
the order of the Hon’ble Court.
PwC  further  requested  that  any  scrutiny,  review,
consideration,  or  assessment  of  the  report  submitted
28

## Page 49

pursuant to the said order be undertaken exclusively by the
Hon’ble Supreme Court of India and that the report not be
challenged  before  any  other  court  or  quasi-judicial
authority.
The aforesaid request is placed before the Hon’ble
Court for its consideration and appropriate orders.
2. Disclaimer, Retention of Documents and Invoicing
A. Disclaimer [Paragraph 3(C) of the Terms of Reference]
PwC clarified that the report would be prepared solely on
the basis of the data and documents furnished by the
Company, Unitech Ltd. (Respondent). PwC stated that it would
not independently verify the authenticity or veracity of the
data and documents furnished by the Company or independently
ascertain the accuracy of the facts stated therein.
PwC requested that the aforesaid limitation regarding
the scope of its examination and verification be taken on
record by the Hon’ble Court and appropriately reflected in
its order.
B. Retention of Documents [Paragraph 3(D) of the Terms of
Reference] PwC expressed the need to retain copies of all
materials and working papers relevant to the preparation of
the report, including materials and documents furnished by
the parties concerned, in accordance with the applicable
Terms of Reference.
After deliberations, it was requested that PwC be
permitted to retain copies of such materials, documents, and
working papers for future reference and record purposes,
subject to the directions of the Hon’ble Court.
C. Invoicing and Disbursement of Fees :  PwC requested
that a single lender be identified against whom the invoice
for its professional fees could be raised.
Alternatively,  it  was  suggested  that  the  lenders
referred to in paragraph 8 of the order dated 27.05.2026
may deposit the requisite fee with the Registry of the

The  aforesaid  proposals  regarding  invoicing  and

1.  This order disposes of Interlocutory Applications regarding claims 
filed by plot holders/allottees of PACL at Sector 100 and 104 of Mohali, 
and at Bhatinda. 
2.  The present dispute arises from the regulatory action taken by the 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (“ SEBI”) against PACL on the 
ground that it s business model , under which it collected money from 
public/investors under various investment schemes, constituted an 
unregistered Collective Investment Scheme (“CIS”).  

## Page 63

 
2 
3.  In 1999, SEBI issued notices directing PACL to either obtain 
registration under the SEBI (CIS) Regulations, 1999, or to wind up its 
operations. Asserting that its activities were confined to real estate 
dealings and did not constitute CIS activity, PACL in itiated writ 
proceedings before the High Court of Rajasthan. By its judgment dated 
28.11.2003, the High Court allowed the said writ petition, holding that 
PACL’s activities did not satisfy the statutory requirements of a CIS, and 
consequently quashed the notices issued by SEBI. In the a ppeal filed by 
SEBI, by its order dated 26.02.2013, this Court disposed of the appeal by 
setting aside the judgment of the High Court and remanded the matter to 
SEBI, directing that the original 1999 notices be treated as show -cause 
notices and that SEBI should conduct a de novo adjudication to determine 
whether its business activities fell within the ambit of a CIS. 
4.  Pursuant to the said remand, SEBI passed final orders concluding 
that PACL was , indeed, running an unregistered CIS and directed its 
promoters and directors to refund the monies collected from investors and 
to wind up all existing schemes. This order was upheld by the Securities 
Appellate Tribunal (SAT). It is in this context that the present Civil Appeals 
against this judgment and order of SAT are ongoing.  
5.  By an order dated 02.02.2016, this Court constituted the Justice 
(Retd.) R.M. Lodha Committee ( “the Committee”), which was entrusted 
with the dual mandate of liquidating the Company ’s land assets and 

## Page 64

 
3 
ensuring the equitable refund of investor funds. In furtherance of these 
duties, the Committee retrieved and scrutinized title deeds from the CBI, 
engaged necessary experts for valuation and auditing, and also 
formulated and executed modalities for the sal e of immovable properties 
and then verified and disbursed investors’ claims. 
6.  The Committee’s proposal for appointment of Shri R. S. Virk, District 
Judge (Retd.) , to examine a large number of applications, objections, 
grievances, and representations related to Committee’s proceedings was 
accepted by this Court’s order dated 15.11.2017. Subsequently, m any 
such applications were heard and disposed by Shri R.S. Virk following due 
procedure. In the course of these proceedings, a large number of 
Interlocutory Applications (IAs) were filed by various parties before us. 
7.  For the purpose of disposal of the present IAs it may be stated that 
the Committee examined the records relating to the residential projects 
that PACL had at Sectors 100 and 104, Mohali, and at Bhatinda. The 
Committee found that Sectors 100 and 104 at Mohali, together, had 2032 
units and Bhatinda had 1078 units, and that many were allotted or sold 
before 02.02.2016.  
8.   By order dated 04.03.2020 , this Court, while consider ing I.A No. 
150831 of 2023 (filed by State of Punjab) and I.A No. 105681 of 2019 
(filed by Pearl City Mohali Residents Welfare Association), directed 
disclosure of the names of the allottees of plots in Sectors 100 and 104 in 

## Page 65

 
4 
Mohali, the dates on which the respective agreements were entered into , 
the mode and dates of payment, and whether the original allottees remain 
members of the Association or have transferred their rights.  Pearl City 
Mohali Residents Welfare Association filed an affidavit dated 04.10.2024, 
supplying the necessary details regarding allottees of Sector 100 and 104, 
Mohali. By order dated 17.10.2024 , this Court asked the Committee to 
verify the claims with the assistance of an auditor.   
9.   Thereafter, the Committee, after duly considering the claims with the 
assistance of chartered accountants, filed a Final Report on 28.02.2025. 
After having considered the matter, this Court, by its Order dated 
02.04.2025, requested the Committee to suggest  a further course of 
action.  
10.  Accordingly, t he Committe e, in its report dated 19.04.2025 (“the 
Report”), analysed all the claims, categorised  them into five categories 
and made re commendations in respect of each category . The learned

counsel, assisted by Ms. Nupur Kumar, learned counsel, have collated a 
Note dated 08.10.2026 (“Amici Note”) , which sets out the categories, 
further course of action  and the number of allottees in each category, in 
the following manner –

13.  We will now proceed to consider the recommendations of the

A.   Categories I – Full Payment through banking channels  
14.   Category I members  are those who  have either ( i) made full 
payment through bank channels and have possession certificate issued, 
or, (ii) made full payment through banking channels but have not received 
a possession certificate nor was the sale deed executed. Of this category, 
the 92 allottees in Sector 100, Mohali are mentioned at Annexure 1, 241 
allottees in Sector 104, Mohali mentioned at Annexure 4 and 203 allottees 
in Bhatinda mentioned at Annexure 7. The Report dated 19.04.2025 
recommended that plots/allotments to allottees in Category I be treated 
as sold and that the necessary sale certificate/NOC be issued to them.  
15.  Accepting the recommendation, we issue the following directions –  
i.  We hereby direct that sale certificates/no objection certificates 
be issued by the Recovery Officer under Section 28A of the SEBI Act  to 
each of these allottees as mentioned in Annexures 1, 4, and 7 within 8 
weeks from today.  
ii.  We also direct the Recovery Officer to give the necessary 
possession certificate to those in limb (ii) of the Category I within the same 
time period.

22.  We have duly considered the submissions made on behalf of the 
Category III allottees as well as the alternatives suggested by the learned 
Amici. The Supreme Court is exercising extraordinary jurisdiction that it 
has assumed in 2016. More than a decade has passed since then , and 
yet, this Court has been struggling to resolve this issue. Committees have 
been constituted , and various reports have been submitted and 
 
5 IA No. 114869 of 2025.  

## Page 78

 
17 
considered sporadically, within the limited time this Court has. These 
proceedings are not in the context of regular original or appellate 
jurisdiction that this Court exercises. It is necessary for this Court to 
conclude these proceedings at the earliest and at the same time , ensure 
that the investors are restituted in a reasonable manner. We cannot afford 
to convert these proceedings into suits for specific performance or public 
law proceedings for restitution and rehabilitation. Taking a practical and 
pragmatic view, it is necessary to take difficult decisions to ensure that the 
monies paid are returned with reasonable interest. The primary obligation 
in the present proceedings is to secure, to the extent possible, the return 
of monies to persons whose claims have been duly examined and verified 
by the Committee.  
23.  Further, this Court cannot afford to complicate the process  of 
securing at least the repayment of the monies invested by the applicants, 
together with reasonable interest, by attempting to devise mechanisms for 
the fulfilment of their original commercial transactions. Such an exercise 
may, in fact, leave the respondents without even recovering the monies 
they paid. Having regard to the considerable passage of time , this Court 
cannot hazard a probable relief where plans and directions to make 
balance payments, resolution of existing claims and disputes over title, 
transfer of unencumbered property , and creation of fresh title, will all 
happen with certainty. The best this Court can do now is conclude the 

## Page 79

 
18 
proceedings and ensure that the applicants are repaid the monies they 
invested, with reasonable interest.  
24.  In view of the above, we accept and adopt the suggestion (iii) of the 
Amici Note and issue the following directions -  
i.  The Committee is directed to refund to each allottee under this 
Category, as mentioned in Annexure 3, 6 and 9, the amount paid by them, 
as certified by the auditors and recorded in the Report, with interest at the 
rate of 8%.    
ii.  The refund, together with the interest payable, shall be made 
within three months from the date of successful auction of the concerned 
plot.  
iii.  Upon payment of the aforesaid amount, the claim of the 
concerned allottee in respect of the plot shall stand fully satisfied, and no 
further claim in relation to such allotment shall survive.

29.2  Transactions which have been acknowledged by PACL,

29.3 They propose that their claims be determined by a Retired Judge or

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. IA No.167477/2026 (application for intervention) is allowed.
The applicant(s) is permitted to intervene in the matter.
2. With  reference  to  the  various  suggestions  made  and
consequential directions proposed by the learned Amicus Curiae in
her Note dated 14.10.2026, the learned Attorney General for India
has placed on record a Note dated 28.10.2026, suggesting certain
directions on behalf of the Union of India.
3. While we are inclined to issue appropriate directions, having
regard to the suggestions made by the learned Amicus Curiae as well
as the Union of India, we consider it appropriate, in the first
instance, to examine the Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer)
Amendment Directions, 2026, which are proposed to be notified by
30.11.2026 and operationalized by 31.12.2026.
4. We  reiterate  and  emphasize  that  the  regulatory  measures
proposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate and
incorporate suitable provisions that require financial institutions
to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds
and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the
customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred
due to the failure on the part of the financial institution to
exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident.
5. We  have  also  emphasised  in  the  past  various  preventive
safeguards that must be mandated for every financial institution.
12

## Page 140

These may include temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious
transactions  inconsistent  with  the  account's  past  transaction
history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest
police station, and subsequently physically verifying the reported
transactions to ascertain their genuineness.
6. In order to ensure effective implementation of the regulatory
measures proposed by the RBI, as well as the directions issued by
us, we further direct the RBI to submit a list of all the
authorized financial institutions before this court on the next
date of hearing.
7. Meanwhile, we also direct all the Law Enforcement Agencies in
States and Union Territories to submit the status of the FIRs
registered thus far in connection with digital arrest scam cases
and the resultant investigation undertaken. They shall also suggest
appropriate measures for the prevention, detection and prosecution
of such cases. The Directors General of Police of all States and
Union Territories shall ensure compliance with these directions.
The information furnished to this Court shall simultaneously be
forwarded to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).
8. WhatsApp  LLC  (A  Meta  Company)  and  other  concerned
intermediaries are also directed to apprise this Court of the
measures they propose to undertake to prevent the digital arrest
scams and related cybercrimes. They shall also simultaneously
submit their proposals to the I4C.
9. Post this matter for further consideration on 23.11.2026.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. IA No.167477/2026 (application for intervention) is allowed.
The applicant(s) is permitted to intervene in the matter.
2. With  reference  to  the  various  suggestions  made  and
consequential directions proposed by the learned Amicus Curiae in
her Note dated 14.10.2026, the learned Attorney General for India
has placed on record a Note dated 28.10.2026, suggesting certain
directions on behalf of the Union of India.
3. While we are inclined to issue appropriate directions, having
regard to the suggestions made by the learned Amicus Curiae as well
as the Union of India, we consider it appropriate, in the first
instance, to examine the Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer)
Amendment Directions, 2026, which are proposed to be notified by
30.11.2026 and operationalized by 31.12.2026.
4. We  reiterate  and  emphasize  that  the  regulatory  measures
proposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate and
incorporate suitable provisions that require financial institutions
to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds
and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the
customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred
due to the failure on the part of the financial institution to
exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident.
5. We  have  also  emphasised  in  the  past  various  preventive
safeguards that must be mandated for every financial institution.
25

## Page 153

These may include temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious
transactions  inconsistent  with  the  account's  past  transaction
history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest
police station, and subsequently physically verifying the reported
transactions to ascertain their genuineness.
6. In order to ensure effective implementation of the regulatory
measures proposed by the RBI, as well as the directions issued by
us, we further direct the RBI to submit a list of all the
authorized financial institutions before this court on the next
date of hearing.
7. Meanwhile, we also direct all the Law Enforcement Agencies in
States and Union Territories to submit the status of the FIRs
registered thus far in connection with digital arrest scam cases
and the resultant investigation undertaken. They shall also suggest
appropriate measures for the prevention, detection and prosecution
of such cases. The Directors General of Police of all States and
Union Territories shall ensure compliance with these directions.
The information furnished to this Court shall simultaneously be
forwarded to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).
8. WhatsApp  LLC  (A  Meta  Company)  and  other  concerned
intermediaries are also directed to apprise this Court of the
measures they propose to undertake to prevent the digital arrest
scams and related cybercrimes. They shall also simultaneously
submit their proposals to the I4C.
9. Post this matter for further consideration on 23.11.2026.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. IA No.167477/2026 (application for intervention) is allowed.
The applicant(s) is permitted to intervene in the matter.
2. With  reference  to  the  various  suggestions  made  and
consequential directions proposed by the learned Amicus Curiae in
her Note dated 14.10.2026, the learned Attorney General for India
has placed on record a Note dated 28.10.2026, suggesting certain
directions on behalf of the Union of India.
3. While we are inclined to issue appropriate directions, having
regard to the suggestions made by the learned Amicus Curiae as well
as the Union of India, we consider it appropriate, in the first
instance, to examine the Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer)
Amendment Directions, 2026, which are proposed to be notified by
30.11.2026 and operationalized by 31.12.2026.
4. We  reiterate  and  emphasize  that  the  regulatory  measures
proposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate and
incorporate suitable provisions that require financial institutions
to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds
and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the
customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred
due to the failure on the part of the financial institution to
exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident.
5. We  have  also  emphasised  in  the  past  various  preventive
safeguards that must be mandated for every financial institution.
12

## Page 166

These may include temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious
transactions  inconsistent  with  the  account's  past  transaction
history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest
police station, and subsequently physically verifying the reported
transactions to ascertain their genuineness.
6. In order to ensure effective implementation of the regulatory
measures proposed by the RBI, as well as the directions issued by
us, we further direct the RBI to submit a list of all the
authorized financial institutions before this court on the next
date of hearing.
7. Meanwhile, we also direct all the Law Enforcement Agencies in
States and Union Territories to submit the status of the FIRs
registered thus far in connection with digital arrest scam cases
and the resultant investigation undertaken. They shall also suggest
appropriate measures for the prevention, detection and prosecution
of such cases. The Directors General of Police of all States and
Union Territories shall ensure compliance with these directions.
The information furnished to this Court shall simultaneously be
forwarded to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).
8. WhatsApp  LLC  (A  Meta  Company)  and  other  concerned
intermediaries are also directed to apprise this Court of the
measures they propose to undertake to prevent the digital arrest
scams and related cybercrimes. They shall also simultaneously
submit their proposals to the I4C.
9. Post this matter for further consideration on 23.11.2026.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. IA No.167477/2026 (application for intervention) is allowed.
The applicant(s) is permitted to intervene in the matter.
2. With  reference  to  the  various  suggestions  made  and
consequential directions proposed by the learned Amicus Curiae in
her Note dated 14.10.2026, the learned Attorney General for India
has placed on record a Note dated 28.10.2026, suggesting certain
directions on behalf of the Union of India.
3. While we are inclined to issue appropriate directions, having
regard to the suggestions made by the learned Amicus Curiae as well
as the Union of India, we consider it appropriate, in the first
instance, to examine the Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer)
Amendment Directions, 2026, which are proposed to be notified by
30.11.2026 and operationalized by 31.12.2026.
4. We  reiterate  and  emphasize  that  the  regulatory  measures
proposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate and
incorporate suitable provisions that require financial institutions
to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds
and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the
customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred
due to the failure on the part of the financial institution to
exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident.
5. We  have  also  emphasised  in  the  past  various  preventive
safeguards that must be mandated for every financial institution.
25

## Page 179

These may include temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious
transactions  inconsistent  with  the  account's  past  transaction
history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest
police station, and subsequently physically verifying the reported
transactions to ascertain their genuineness.
6. In order to ensure effective implementation of the regulatory
measures proposed by the RBI, as well as the directions issued by
us, we further direct the RBI to submit a list of all the
authorized financial institutions before this court on the next
date of hearing.
7. Meanwhile, we also direct all the Law Enforcement Agencies in
States and Union Territories to submit the status of the FIRs
registered thus far in connection with digital arrest scam cases
and the resultant investigation undertaken. They shall also suggest
appropriate measures for the prevention, detection and prosecution
of such cases. The Directors General of Police of all States and
Union Territories shall ensure compliance with these directions.
The information furnished to this Court shall simultaneously be
forwarded to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).
8. WhatsApp  LLC  (A  Meta  Company)  and  other  concerned
intermediaries are also directed to apprise this Court of the
measures they propose to undertake to prevent the digital arrest
scams and related cybercrimes. They shall also simultaneously
submit their proposals to the I4C.
9. Post this matter for further consideration on 23.11.2026.

   UPON hearing the counsels, the Court made the following
                             
O R D E R
1. These special leave petitions are by a variety of
teachers appointed in the State of Tripura pursuant
to advertisements issued in 2002, 2006 and 2009. A
challenge was laid to the education policy prevailing
3

## Page 223

in the State as also to the method of selection
adopted for making appointment of teachers in the
State which came to be addressed by the High Court of
Tripura (for short, the High Court) in Tanmoy Nath
and Others Vs. State of Tripura and others, (2014) 2
TLR 731. 
2. The High Court by its detailed judgment and order
dated 07.05.2014 held the policy bad in law and
entire  selection  made  thereunder  pursuant  to  the
aforesaid advertisements involving appointments of
10,323 teachers was set aside. The operative portion
of the order of the High Court is found in paragraphs
121, 122, 123 and 124 of the judgment which are
reproduced hereinbelow: 
121. It has been urged that even if we set
aside the selections, our judgment should
be prospective in nature. It has also been
urged  by  Mr.  Sankar  Deb,  learned  Sr.
Counsel  for  the  petitioners,  that  those
portions of the policy which are bad may be
severed and those portions which can be
upheld  may  be  retained,  but  the
appointments  already  made  need  not  be
disturbed. Reliance has been placed on the
judgments of the Apex Court in A.P. Public
Service Commission v. K. Sudharshan Reddy
and others, (2006) 5 SCC 505, AIR 1957 SC
628, (2000) 7 SCC 719. These judgments have
no applicability to the cases in hand and
we  are  not  all  in  agreement  with  this
submission.  The  selections  have  been
totally  unfair.  The  selections  have  not
been  made  in  a  transparent  manner.  The
citizens  of  this  country  have  not  been
treated equally. Most of the clauses of the
policy  are  illegal  and  unconstitutional.
The entire policy is bad because it gives
no guidelines and, therefore, the entire
4

## Page 224

selection will have to be, must be and is
accordingly set aside. 
122.  Though  we  have  set  aside  the
selections,  we  are  concerned  with  the
education of the small children who are
innocent  and  have  no  concern  with  the
illegalities  of  the  selection.  We,
therefore, direct that the teachers whose
selections  have  been  set  aside  shall
continue to function in their present place
of postings till 31-12-2014, i.e. the end
of the academic session of this year.
123. The State on or before 31-12-2014 must
complete a fresh process of selection of
teachers in all categories. In view of the
discussions held above, we direct that the
State should frame a new Employment Policy
within two months from today and shall
carry out selections in accordance with the
fresh policy as early as possible and not
later than 31-12-2014.
124. It is not for this Court to frame
guidelines but if the State does not frame
any guidelines, then the State shall follow
the  following  directions  while  making
selections. If the State frames its own
guidelines, it must ensure that they are in
tune with the law laid down by the Apex
Court as discussed by us above and in light
of the directions given hereinafter.
(i) Fresh applications shall be invited
for  all  the  posts;
(ii) Even those who have applied earlier
will have to apply again though they may
be given relaxation in age and no fees
may be charged from them;
(iii) The State shall clearly set out the
number  of  posts  in  each  category  of
teachers;
(iv) In case of undergraduate teachers,
the State if it is so advised may divide
the posts sub-division wise so that the
primary school teachers are local people
as far as possible;
5

## Page 225

(v) In respect of graduate teachers, the
State may divide the posts district wise;
(vi) In case of postgraduate teachers,
there will be no zone wise division of
posts;
(vii) In case the State decides to make
division  of  posts  region  wise,  as
indicate hereinabove, then the candidates
must be asked to apply only for one
region of their choice. It should also be
specified in the advertisements that once
a candidate applies under any category
then he shall not be permitted to change
his category and the roll number should
be allocated in such a fashion that the
category and region of each candidate is
clearly  depicted  in  the  roll  number
itself.
(viii) For each category of teachers, a
written  test  preferably  an  objective
(MCQ) test must be held;
(ix) This test should be conducted by an
independent body like the Tripura Public
Service Commission or the Tripura Central
University;
(x) The test should be multiple choice
question and the answer sheet should be
checked through a computer keeping in
view  the  large  number  of  candidates
involved;
(xi) At least 50% of the total marks
shall be awarded on the basis of the
performance in the written test, i.e. in
case a candidate obtains 70 marks out of
100 in a written test, 35 marks out of 50
shall be awarded to him towards the total
assessment;
(xii).  In  the  case  of  Post  Graduate
Teachers  another  20  marks  shall  be
awarded for the marks received in the
qualifying course, i.e. B.A./B.Sc./B.Com
(Honours)  or  post-graduation,  i.e.
6

## Page 226

M.A./M.Sc./M.Com.  Therefore,  if  a
candidate has obtained 50% marks in the
qualifying course, he would get 10 out of
20 under this head. A candidate, who has
higher qualifications, for example he is
an Hons. Graduate and has also done his
post-graduation or has done his post-
graduation in 2(two) subjects, then he
may be awarded 5 more. Similarly 5 more
marks  shall  be  awarded  to  those
candidates who have obtained Ph. D. or
similar qualifications. Since consistency
has an important role, 5 marks each i.e.
10 marks shall be awarded for the marks
obtained  in  Madhyamik  and  Higher
Secondary  examination  respectively.
Therefore, if a candidate has 40% marks
in Madhyamik he will get 2 out of 5 and
if he has 60% marks in Higher Secondary
he will get 3 marks. Out of the remaining
10 marks which shall be awarded at the
time  of  interview  5  marks  shall  be
earmarked for extra-curricular activities
i.e. sports, music, drama or NCC etc. but
the  State  must  lay  down  clear-cut
guidelines as to how these marks have to
be  allotted.  Therefore,  the  interview
board will have the liberty to award 5
marks on the basis of oral interview.
(xiii). In case of Graduate Teachers, 50%
marks  shall  be  allocated  for  the
performance  in  the  written  test,  20%
marks  for  the  marks  obtained  in  the
qualifying  course  i.e.  Graduation,  5
marks on the basis of marks obtained in
Higher Secondary and 5 marks for the
marks obtained in Madhyamik and 10 marks
shall  be  awarded  on  the  basis  of
percentage of marks for candidates when
done post graduate. Similarly, Out of the
remaining 10 marks which shall be awarded
at the time of interview 5 marks shall be
earmarked for extra-curricular activities
i.e. sports, music, drama or NCC etc. and
5 for performance in interview.
(xiv). For Under Graduate Teachers 50%
shall be allocated for performance in the
written test, 10 marks for the marks
obtained in Madhyamik, 10 marks for the
marks obtained in Higher Secondary and 15
marks  shall  be  awarded  to  those
candidates who are qualified as per the
7

## Page 227

NET guidelines i.e. they have passed TET
or B. Ed or 2(two) years Diploma in
Teaching.  5  Marks  for  higher
qualifications. Out of the remaining 10
marks which shall be awarded at the time
of interview 5 marks shall be earmarked
for  extra-curricular  activities  i.e.
sports, music, drama or NCC etc. and 5
for performance in interview.
(xv). We may make it clear that 50% seats
shall be filled in only on the basis of
merit.  In  the  State  of  Tripura  the
reservation is as follows:
Scheduled  Tribe  -  31%
Scheduled  Caste  -  17%
General  Category  -  52%
Therefore, if there are 1000 posts in a
particular  category  of  'Teachers'  at
least  165  Scheduled  Tribe  candidates
should be selected on the basis of merit
amongst Scheduled Tribes, 85 candidates
belonging to Scheduled Castes be selected
on the basis of merit drawn out amongst
the Scheduled Caste category and 260 out
of the unreserved/general category shall
be appointed strictly on the basis of
merit drawn out as above.
(xvi). The State must also ensure that in
accordance  with  the  Persons  with
Disability Act and the law laid down by
the Apex Court in a number of cases
including Union of India and Anr. Vs.
National  Federation  of  the  Blind  and
Ors., [(2013)10 SCC 772] adequate numbers
of posts are reserved for persons with
disabilities.
(xvii). In case the States so desires, it
may reserve a small percentage of posts
for Ex-servicemen or wards of those who
have died fighting for the Country or
have been severely disabled. However, the
reservation  under  this  head  shall  be
horizontal and not above 5%. The number
of posts in this category should also be
8

## Page 228

clearly defined.
(xviii). The State may, if it so desires,
also out of this 50% give some weightage
to persons who have been waiting for the
appointment for a long time. Therefore,
there can be additional 20 marks to be
awarded for seniority i.e. 1 mark for
each  year  of seniority  subject  to  a
maximum of 20 marks. Similarly, the State
may also give some weightage to members
of the needy families out of these 50%
posts and may allot 10 marks for those
persons  who  belonged  to  the  needy
category. Therefore, the remaining 50% of
posts the marking may be out of 130 i.e.
20 marks for seniority and 10 marks for
need.
(xix). Effectively, those selected only
on the basis of the merit shall be graded
out of a maximum of 100 marks but for
those who are given benefit of seniority
and/or belonging to a poor family the
marking will be out of 130 marks. It is,
however, made clear that the State at the
time of framing of the policy shall also
lay down clear-cut guidelines how the
needy families are to be identified.
(i) The identification must be done on
clearly set out criteria i.e. to say the
upper  income  limit  should  be  clearly
defined.
(ii) It should be clearly stated that no
member  of  the  family  should  be  in
government/organized employment.
(iii) It should be clearly stated that
the land of the family should be below a
certain area.
We  also  make  it  clear  that  any
certificate given to a person said to be
needy  can  be  challenged  by  the
9

## Page 229

unsuccessful candidates if they feel that
this certificate has been wrongly given.
125. We would also like to make it clear
that other than the benefits indicated by
US  above  there  can  be  no
reservation/preference on the basis of
age. There shall be no preference to
dependent government servants or retired
government  employee  or  retrenched
employees  etc.  There  can  be  no
reservation for linguistic or religious
minorities or on area wise basis. It is
further made clear that if the persons
who  are  selected  in  the  previous
selection are again selected then the
service rendered by them earlier shall be
counted for the purpose of seniority,
pension and all other purposes.
3. The order of the High Court was challenged before
this  Court  by  the  State  of  Tripura  and  others
affected. However, those petitions were disposed of
by this Court vide order dated 29.03.2017, which is
reproduced below:
“We have heard learned counsel for the
parties and perused the record. We do
not find any ground to interfere with
the impugned order. 
While setting aside the selections, the
High Court in Para 123 of the impugned
order observed: 
   “123.  The  State  on  or  before
31.12.2014  must  complete  a  fresh
process of selection of teachers in
all  categories.  In  view  of  the
discussions  held  above,  we  direct
that the State should frame a new
Employment Policy within two months
from  today  and  shall  carry  out
selections  in  accordance  with  the
fresh policy as early as possible and
not later than 31.12.2014.” 
While  issuing  notice  in  the  present
10

## Page 230

matters this Court by its order dated
04.08.2014  stayed  the  directions
contained in aforesaid para 123 of the
impugned order. Since we do not find any
ground to interfere with the impugned
order, the directions in para 123 now
required to be suitably modified. We,
therefore, direct: 
(a) New  Employment  Policy  should  be
framed by the State by 30th April,
2017  if  not  already  framed  and
advertisements for filling up the
vacancies may be issued latest by
31st, May, 2017. 
(b) The  fresh  selection  process  be
completed  on  or  before  31st
December, 2017 and till the fresh
process is completed, the teachers
already appointed shall continue. 
(c) The candidates who participated in
the selection process pursuant to
the  advertisements  in  question,
whether selected or not, will be
allowed to participate in the fresh
selection process by relaxing their
age but subject to their having
necessary qualifications.
(d) The qualifications in the case of
teachers governed by the provisions
of the Right of Children to Free
and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
shall be in conformity with the
relevant  statutory  provisions  of
the said Act.
(e) The  qualifications  of  teachers
employed for Classes IX and above
shall  be  strictly  in  compliance
with  the  relevant  provisions
concerning such appointments.
Subject to the aforesaid modifications,
the view taken by the High Court in the
impugned  order  is  affirmed  and  the
special leave petitions are dismissed. 
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  also
stand disposed of.”
11

## Page 231

4. The direction contained in clause (b) qua continuance
of teachers whose appointments were set aside was
modified from time to time and the period up to which
they could continue was extended up to 31.03.2020.
After expiry of the aforesaid period, those teachers
were served termination orders. Those termination
orders were separately challenged by such teachers
through  separate  writ  petitions  before  the  High
Court. The High Court by separate impugned orders has
dismissed those writ petitions as well as the writ
appeals. In consequence, those writ petitioners are
before this Court through separate petitions seeking
leave to appeal. 
5. At this stage, we may also notice that on the subject
qua the termination of appointment of such teachers
there  were  conflicting  views  taken  by  coordinate
benches of the High Court and, therefore, the matter
was referred to the full Bench of the High Court
which ultimately, vide its judgment dated 26.09.2023,
settled  the  law  holding  that  the  judgment  would
operate in rem binding all teachers appointed under
those advertisements. 
6. The points urged before the High Court as well as
before  us  on  behalf  of  different  categories  of
teachers (i.e., writ petitioners) are as follows:
12

## Page 232

(1) The writ petitioners were not party to the
proceedings in which the decision in  Tanmoy
Nath (supra)  was  rendered,  therefore,  the
decision in Tanmoy Nath (supra) does not bind
them. Besides, once appointed, their services
cannot be terminated except by following a
procedure known to law.
(2) Tanmoy  Nath (supra)  dealt  with  a
challenge  to  the  education  policy  whereas
appointments were made under the extant rules
and,  therefore,  even  if  the  policy  is
annulled  or  set  aside,  individual
appointments would not be affected.
(3) The judgment in Tanmoy Nath (supra) dealt
with graduate teachers and would, therefore,
not  include  teachers  falling  in  other
category i.e. Post Graduate Teachers.
7. It is the case of the petitioners that the High
Court has not properly addressed the points urged
before it. The High Court wrongly took the view
that since in the lead petition of  Tanmoy Nath
(supra)  a  public  notice  was  issued  inviting
intervention applications from all those who might
be  affected  by  the  order  of  the  High  Court,
individual  notices  were  not  required  to  each
appointee. It is also the case of the petitioners
that  in  absence  of  individual  notice  to  each
appointee, the appointees were deprived of putting
their case before the High Court justifying the
procedure adopted in their appointment.  
8. It was also urged that the order of the High Court
13

## Page 233

in Tanmoy Nath (supra) determined the validity of
education policy and not the extant rules under
which the appointments were to be made pursuant to
the advertisements.  Therefore, where appointments
were made following the extant Regulations/Rules,
those appointments could not have been annulled by
a sweeping order wherein writ petitioners were not
parties. 
9. In addition to above, by relying on paragraph 127
of the judgment in Tanmoy Nath (supra), it has been
urged that the order in Tanmoy Nath (supra) did not
intend to disturb existing appointments. In such
circumstances, it is urged, the petitioners who had
served for over a decade were not liable to be
terminated pursuant to the general direction given
in Tanmoy Nath (supra), which was affirmed by this
Court.
10. Per  contra,  Ms.  Divan,  Senior  Advocate,  who  has
appeared for the State, submitted that the decision
in Tanmoy Nath (supra) is an order in rem which would
operate on all appointees appointed pursuant to the
recruitment exercise initiated under the recruitment
advertisements in question. It is not in dispute that
all writ petitioners who are before this Court were
appointed pursuant to the exercise initiated under
those recruitment notifications and, therefore, all
14

## Page 234

such appointments would have to abide by the order
passed in Tanmoy Nath (supra) which has been affirmed
by this Court. It has also been urged that a close
reading of the order in  Tanmoy Nath (supra) would
indicate that it does not merely deals with the
education policy but also the manner in which the
selections were to be made under that policy. The
High  Court  noticed  that  there  were  insufficient
guidelines  qua the  procedure  to  be  adopted  for
appointment which vitiated the entire selection and
consequential  appointments,  therefore,  the  Court
deemed it appropriate to declare entire selection
pursuant to those advertisements as void. It has also
been  submitted  that  individual  notices  were  not
required inasmuch as notice was published through
newspaper publication inviting intervention by all
such teachers who were appointed pursuant to the
recruitment  exercise  initiated  under  the
advertisements. In such circumstances, once it is not
in dispute that all writ petitioners before this
Court had been appointed under those advertisements,
selection whereunder has been set aside by the order
of the High Court, affirmed by this Court, no relief
can be granted to such petitioners. 
11.We  have  accorded  due  consideration  to  the  rival
contentions and have carefully perused the orders
15

## Page 235

passed by the High Court in Tanmoy Nath (supra) and
the order passed by this Court affirming the said
order as well as the subsequent orders which were
passed from time to time raising similar issues. It
can be noticed from those orders and in particular
the order of this Court in Civil Appeal No.2868 of
2020 filed by Ajoy Debbarma and others that selection
of 10,323 teachers made by the Government of Tripura
pursuant to advertisements issued in 2002, 2006 and
2009 was subject matter of challenge before the High
Court of Tripura in  Tanmoy Nath (supra) and the
challenge was accepted by the High Court on the
ground that selection was contrary to the provisions
of the National Council for Teacher Education Act,
1993 and the relevant policies and those appointments
were arbitrary and illegal. This Court also noticed
that the decision in Tanmoy Nath (supra) had attained
finality upon being affirmed by this Court. 
12.It is clear from the order of this Court dated
29.03.2017 that the candidates who had participated
in  the  selection  process  pursuant  to  the
advertisements in question, whether selected or not,
were  to be  allowed to  participate in  the fresh
selection process by relaxing their age but subject
to their having necessary qualifications. Further, it
was directed that fresh selection process had to be
16

## Page 236

completed by a specified date and only till the
process is completed the teachers already appointed
were to continue. From above, it is manifestly clear
that entire selection and consequential appointments
under those advertisements stood annulled and a fresh
recruitment exercise had to be undertaken. No doubt
fresh recruitment exercise could not be completed by
or  before  31.12.2017,  but  this  period  has  been
extended from time to time and all those who were
appointed were allowed to continue up to 31.03.2020.
Admittedly,  the  aforesaid  period  has  not  been
extended beyond 31.03.2020. In such circumstances, if
the services have been terminated in compliance of
the earlier order passed in  Tanmoy Nath which has
been affirmed by this Court, no fault can be found
with such orders.  In our view, the writ petitions
were rightly dismissed.  
13.The  argument  that  the  orders  did  not  relate  to
teachers already appointed is completely misconceived
as paragraph 127 of Tanmoy Nath judgment has rightly
been interpreted as being confined to non-teachers.
The other argument that Tanmoy Nath would not apply
to all category of teachers is equally misconceived
as it covers entire selection of teachers under those
advertisements.
14.The special leave petitions have, therefore, no merit
17

## Page 237

and are, therefore, dismissed.
15.All pending applications as well as applications for
impleadment / intervention / modification shall stand
disposed of.

SLP (C) No. 36131/2026
1.  We have heard Advocate Sanchar Anand, appearing for the
petitioner  and  Advocate  Aruna  Sachdeva,  appearing  for  the
respondents.
2. The undisputed circumstance is that the first respondent has
been working with the petitioner since 1993. Through the order
dated  15.01.2026  in  C.W.P.  No.  9942  of  2005,  the  following
directions were issued by the learned Single Judge:
“14. The  respondents  are  directed  to  regularize  the
services of the petitioner as Assistant Pump Operator
within  six  weeks  from  today.  If  no  order  of
regularization is passed within 6 weeks from today, he
shall be deemed to be regularized. The petitioner shall
be entitled to counting of past service and other
benefits as per judgments rendered by this Court in
Manjeet Singh and Hari Ram (supra), Harbans Lal v. State
of Punjab, CWP No.2371 of 2010 and State of Haryana and
others v. Jai Bhagwan, LPA No. 1892 of 2019.
15. Pending miscellaneous application(s), if any, be
also disposed of accordingly.”
3. Challenging the order dated 15.01.2026, Letter Patent Appeal
(LPA) was preferred and the LPA has been ordered in terms of the
decision dated 10.07.2026 in Municipal Council Malerkotla.

## Page 255

7
SLP(C) No.35500/2026
4. Hence, the present Special Leave Petition.
5. In the instance of Municipal Council Malerkotla, through the
impugned judgment, the Division Bench directed as follows:
“3. Learned counsel for the appellant(s) submits that
the issue raised in the present appeals has already been
decided by this Court while deciding  LPA No. 1065 of
2026 titled as ‘Municipal Council Malerkotla though its
Executive Officer vs. Kuldeep Singh and Others’ on
10.07.2026 and the present appeals be also dismissed in
same terms.
4. Ordered accordingly.”
6. Learned counsel for the petitioner argues that the judgment
relied upon by the Division Bench is not applicable in all force,
as the decision dated  10.07.2026 directs the payment of pension
through a pension scheme that was discontinued as early as 2004.
Further, the regularization of the first respondent is unavailable
and the first respondent is not qualified to hold the post of Pump
Operator.
7. Advocate  Aruna  Sachdeva,  appearing  for  first  respondent,
argues that the regularization is not for Pump Operator but the
direction is to regularize the services of first respondent as
Assistant Pump Operator. The first respondent is qualified to hold
the post and discharge its functions.
8. Advocate Aruna Sachdeva states that the first respondent may
have difficulty in sustaining the relief to the limited extent of
directing payment of pension under Old Pension Scheme, i.e. General
Provident Fund (GPF) Scheme, which was discontinued in 2004.

## Page 256

8
SLP(C) No.35500/2026
9. We take note of the admitted circumstances and also the
limited issue presented for our consideration.
10. Prima facie, we are of the view that the first respondent is
entitled to the relief of regularization, and to that extent, the
order dated 15.01.2026 in C.W.P. No. 9942/2005 is sustained.
11. With a view to balancing and working out the relief between
the parties, we direct that the services of first respondent be
regularized as Assistant Pump Operator with effect from 01.01.2012
and the first respondent will be on probation for a period of three
years and he shall be deemed to have completed the probation on
31.12.2015.
12. The petitioner is directed to pay the arrears by giving effect
to the regularization as indicated above.
13. Except the relief as granted, the respondent is not entitled
to pension under the Old Pension Scheme.
14. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of as indicated above.
15. It is made clear though the impugned order is passed by
relying upon the decision dated 10.07.2026, having regard to the
circumstances of this case, even if we are partly confirming the
impugned order, the same be understood as having been made in the
circumstances of this case and shall not be treated as a precedent
in any other matter.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 291/2011 
 
 
 
STATE OF U.P. & ORS       APPELLANT(S) 
 
VERSUS 
 
GRAND SLAM FITNESS(P) LTD.            RESPONDENT(S) 
 
WITH 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 293/2011 
 
 
ORDER 
 
 
1. Heard Mr. Bhakti Vardhan Singh and                       
Ms. Charanya Lakshmikumaran, learned counsel for the 
parties. 
2. The respondents in Civil Misc. Writ Petition 
No. 534/2009 and Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 
361/2009 are the appellants. 
3. The Writ Petitioners are private limited 
companies incorporated under the provisions of the 
Companies Act, 1956. They are primarily engaged in 
the sale of physical exercise and fitness equipment, 
such as the Cross Elliptical Trainer, Manual 
Treadmill, Motorized Treadmill, Rowers Exercise 
Bikes, Strength Equipment, etc. The petitioners are 
registered dealers under the U.P. Value Added Tax 
Act, 2008. The companies have filed a Writ of 

## Page 260

2 
Certiorari against the order dated 18.09.2008 passed 
by the second appellant and the order dated 
26.11.2008 passed by the third appellant in the Civil 
Appeals. The subject-matter relates to the period 
from April, 2008 to July, 2008. 
4. Through the order dated 31.10.2008, the 
Revenue called upon the dealers to pay tax @ 12.5% 
under the Act on the sports equipment dealt with by 
the dealers. Here, we use the expression equipment 
inasmuch as the controversy between the Revenue and 
the dealers centres around the nature, name, and code 
entry to which it belongs, and whether the equipment 
dealt with by the dealers falls within the exemption 
granted vide notification dated 09.04.2008. 
5. To appreciate the controversy, the following 
few lines are adverted to: 
5.1 The dealers claim that the equipment falls 
under Commodity Code Entry No. 60 under Section 70 
of the Act under which the goods have been 
classified. The exemption notification dated 
09.04.2008 reads as under: 
“51. Wooden Toys, Lac + Shellac, 
including Paseva Mulamma, Button, Leo and 
Kiri, Sports Goods excluding Apparels, 
and sports Footwear, stop clock. 
A true typed copy of the Notification No. 
1021 dated 9/4 2008 is annexed herewith 
and marked as ANNEXURE P-2 to this SLP.” 

## Page 261

3 
 
6. Therefore, since the equipment dealt with by 
the dealer squarely falls within the definition of 
‘Sports Goods’, first, the levy and imposition of 
tax on exempted goods is impermissible, and second, 
levying tax @ 12.5%, which treats it as unclassified 
goods, is illegal. Hence, prayed for setting aside 
the demand. 
7. The case of Revenue is that the notification 
dated 09.04.2008 employs broad expressions, and from 
the perspective of the revenue, the subsequent 
notification issued would make it clear that, through 
the notification dated 09.04.2008, the revenue did 
not treat the equipment dealt with by the dealer as 
sports goods. Therefore, for the subsequent periods, 
the levy is tenable. 
8. The above controversy has been considered by 
the High Court in the impugned judgment. The High 
Court first referred to Section 70 of the Act and 
the commodity code assigned by the revenue. It is 
not in dispute that Entry No. 60 under the commodity 
codes deals with “sports Goods, Games and Toys”. 
Therefore, the High Court is of the view that there 
is no good or valid reason to exclude the equipment 
dealt with by the dealer from the meaning of sports 
goods. Consequently, the High Court has set aside 

## Page 262

4 
the impugned notice. 
9. The learned counsel appearing for the State 
argues that the High Court ought to have given 
meaning to the expression ‘sports goods’ in relation 
to the notification dated 09.04.2008. Under such an 
understanding, it cannot be said that the equipment 
dealt with by the dealer can be treated as sports 
goods. Therefore, it is argued that the assessments 
dated 18.09.2008 and 26.11.2008 were validly issued 
and that the High Court ought not to have interfered 
with them. 
10. Advocate Charanya Lakshmikumaran, appearing 
for the dealer, contends that the commodity entry is 
general but includes the equipment dealt with by the 
dealer. The reason assigned by the revenue for 
imposing tax @ 12.5% is completely illegal and 
unsustainable. Once the power of the revenue under 
Section 70 of the Act is exercised and the commodity 
code is prepared, denying the benefit of the 
exemption issued through notification dated 
09.04.2008 is illegal. The reasoning of the High 
Court is brief but tenable, and she prays for 
dismissal of the Civil Appeal. 
11. We have taken note of the submissions and 
perused the entries. 
13. Let us first begin with Entry No. 60 (supra), 

## Page 263

5 
which includes sports goods, games and toys. Let us 
juxtapose Entry No. 51 in Schedule-I, amended through 
the notification dated 09.04.2008. The conclusion is 
that the exemption clearly deals with sports goods. 
We have to juxtapose the exemption in the 
notification dated 09.04.2008 with Commodity Code 
No. 60, which deals with sports goods, games and 
toys. A simple juxtaposition of both the entries 
would make it clear that the equipment being dealt 
with by the dealers can be classified as sports 
goods. The impugned order is correct and has applied 
the correct provision of law and the exemption entry. 
14. We see no reason to interfere with the 
impugned order(s).

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.                OF 2026 
(@ SLP (C) No. 31342 of 2025) 
 
MEGHALAYA POWER GENERATION  
CORPORATION LTD.  
(MePGCL)               ….APPELLANT 
 
VERSUS 
 
ODIMAR SYIEMSAD AND ORS.       …RESPONDENTS 
 
O  R  D  E  R 
1. Leave granted. 
2. In this appeal,  the appellant, namely, Meghalaya Power 
Generation Corporation Ltd., a government undertaking (‘the 
Corporation’), has questioned the judgment dated 01.09.2025 
passed by the High Court1 in a Writ Appeal2, insofar as it directs 
the Corporation to pay compensation of Rs. 21,59,242/ - to 
respondent no.1 (‘the unsuccessful bidder’). 
 
1 Division Bench of the High Court of Meghalaya at Shillong 
2 WA No. 36 of 2024 

## Page 269

2 
 
3. Facts giving rise to filing of this appeal in a nutshell are, that on 
04.07.2023, the Corporation issued a notice inviting tenders for 
construction of a multipurpose indoor stadium at Nongtrai Village, 
Mawsynram, East Khasi Hills, at an estimated cost of Rs. 
2,87,89,896/-. In response to the aforesaid tender notice, five 
bidders submitted their bids who were found to be technically 
qualified. On 08.09.2023, the financial bids were opened. Four out 
of five bidders had quoted a sum of Rs. 2,87,89,896/ - and were 
jointly declared lowest bidders, whereas the unsuccessful bidder 
had quoted a sum of Rs. 2,87,89,897.34/ -, that is R upee 1.34 
more and was declared L2.  
4. The Tender Committee, on 07.02.2024, interacted with the lowest 
bidders. Three of the bidders withdrew their bids and consented 
to award the contract in favour of respondent no.2 (‘the successful 
bidder’). On 15.02.2024, a work order was issued in favour of the 
successful bidder. 
5. The unsuccessful bidder filed a writ petition seeking quashing of 
the work order issued in favour of the successful bidder. The 
learned Single Judge vide judgment dated 07.06.2024 recorded a 
finding that lowest bidders had acted in collusion. The learned 

## Page 270

3 
 
Single Judge, therefore, quashed the work order issued in favour 
of the successful bidder and directed a fresh tender. 
6. The Corporation as well as the successful bidder filed intra- court 
appeals before the Division Bench  of the High Court 3. The High 
Court vide judgment dated 01.09.2025 recorded the following 
conclusions: (i) there was not enough evidence to hold that the 
bidders were operating as a cartel, (ii) a proper technical evaluation 
of the bids was conducted, (iii) the T ender Committee was  
theoretically correct in not inviting the unsuccessful bidder in the 
meeting on 07.02.2024  as he was not the lowest bidder  but 
propriety demanded that all the five bidders ought to have been 
called in the meeting , (iv) the tender process may not have been 
perfect but the award of contract to the successful bidder was 
neither illegal nor wrongful,  and (v) no act of impropriety can be 
attributed to members of the Tender Committee. However, the 
High Court held that some injustice has been caused to the 
unsuccessful bidder, and all the five bidders ought to have been 
called to revise their bids and the unsuccessful bidder has been 
 
3 W.A. No. 36 of 2024 and W.A. No. 38 of 2024 

## Page 271

4 
 
deprived of his legitimate expectation of being called for 
negotiations. The High Court on the basis of a decision of this 
Court in A.T. Brij Paul Singh & Bros. v. State of Gujarat4, held 
that profit in a works contract can be estimated at 15% of the value 
of the work. However, t he High Court  awarded the unsuccessful 
bidder compensation at the rate of 7.5% of the value of the work 
and quantified the amount of compensation at Rs. 21,59,242/-. 
7. Being aggrieved, the Corporation is in appeal before us. 
8. Learned counsel for the Corporation submitted that High Court 
even though it did not find any illegality in the tender process, 
grossly erred in awarding compensation in exercise of writ 
jurisdiction. Learned Counsel for successful bidder has supported 
the stand taken by the Corporation. However, despite service of 
notice none has appeared on behalf of the unsuccessful bidder.  
9. We have considered the submissions and have perused the record. 
The direction issued by the High Court to award compensation to 
the unsuccessful bidder cannot be sustained for the following 
reasons: 
 
4 AIR 1984 SC 1703 

## Page 272

5 
 
(i) The direction to pay the compensation is contradictory to the 
finding recorded by the High Court with regard to process of 
tender, especially in view of the following findings: (i) there 
was no cartelization amongst the bidders, (ii) a proper 
technical evaluation of the bids was conducted, (iii) no act of 
impropriety to members of the Tender Committee, and (iv) the 
award of contract to the successful bidder is neither illegal 
nor improper. 
(ii) The finding that all five bidders could have been asked to 
revise their bids, is at best, a view on what might have been 
a better course. It is not a finding of either illegality or 
arbitrariness in the tender process. 
(iii) A bidder has a right to fair consideration of its bid and there 
was no finding that the said right was infringed by the Tender 
Committee. 
(iv) Admittedly, the successful bidder was the lowest tenderer, 
and the unsuccessful bidder could not have any legitimate 
right to be called for negotiation . In any event, even if the 
legitimate expectation of the unsuccessful bidder was 

## Page 273

6 
 
established, it by itself does not give rise to claim for damages 
in a writ petition. 
(v) The High Court travelled beyond the reliefs prayed for in the 
writ petition which was confined only to quashing of the work 
order issued in favour of the successful bidder and erred in 
awarding compensation in a writ proceeding.  
(vi) The High Court ought to have appreciated that no foundation 
for the claim of compensation was laid in the pleadings and 
the Corporation had no occasion to contest the relief granted 
by the High Court. 
(vii) The High Court erred in relying on the decision in A.T Brij 
Paul Singh (supra) and ought to have appreciated that the 
said decision related to claim for damages under Section 73 
of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 for wrongful rescission of a 
concluded works contract where loss of profits was a natural 
consequence of the breach. In the instant case, no contract 
was awarded to the unsuccessful bidder and therefore, there 
was no loss of profit which was capable of assessment. 
(viii) A Writ Court, which finds the decision-making process to be 
valid cannot simultaneously impose monetary liability on a 

## Page 274

7 
 
Government Undertaking on the premise that same process 
has caused injustice to the unsuccessful bidder. 
10. For the aforemen tioned reasons, the impugned judgment dated 
01.09.2025 passed in writ appeal, insofar as it directs payment of 
compensation of Rs. 21,59,242/ - to the unsuccessful bidder, is 
quashed and set aside. The remaining part of the judgment dated 
01.09.2025 is upheld. The successful bidder shall be at liberty to 
proceed in terms of the contract awarded to him.  
11. In the result, the appeal is allowed. There shall be no order as to 
costs. 
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

   UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following

## Page 300

2
                             O R D E R
1. Interim Application No. 353899 of 2026 has been preferred by
the original appellant (Vayu Kishore).
2. In the interim application, the applicant has prayed for the
following:-
“i. Modify the Order dated 04.11.2026 to the extent that it directs
the Appellant herein to extend necessary cooperation required to
ensure that the divorce and custody proceedings are withdrawn
before the US Court;
ii. Modify the Order dated 04.11.2026 to the extent that it directs
the  Appellant  herein  to  avail  no  benefit  from  Order  dated
02.12.2022 passed by the US Court, and that the order is not
pressed or withdrawn by the Appellant; and
iii. Pass any other order or direction that this Hon’ble Court may
deem fit in the interest of justice.”
 
3. The applicant, the original appellant, Vayu Kishore, has given
certain undertakings before this court, as recorded in para 41 of
the main Order dated 8th October, 2026.
4. The undertakings indicate that Vayu Kishore would not only
take care of her daughter, but would also provide for his wife,
that is, the Respondent No.4 - Abhilasha, in various ways including
financial support, accommodation, assistance in obtaining her visa/
getting the Green Card renewed, not pressing or taking coercive
action against her, ensuring that the 50-50 shared parenting
arrangement is followed, and cooperating in any other proceedings
initiated against her in the United States so as to restore family
life. 
5. Further, at the hearing which concluded with the passing of the
Order dated 4th November, 2026, this court was given the impression
that all proceedings, namely the divorce and custody proceedings
before the US Court, and the criminal proceedings, would be
withdrawn, that family life would be restored, and that the parties
would make a fresh start. Further, this Court was also given the
impression that the applicant would not claim any benefit under the
order dated 02.12.2022. Thus, all in all, it was hoped that all

## Page 301

3
past disputes/proceedings/orders would be put to bed and the
Respondent No.4 would have no apprehension in travelling to the US
and starting her life there. 
6. Having regard to the pleadings in the interim application we
are dealing with, and the reliefs prayed for, it appears that this
does not seem to be the intention of the applicant.
7. He now states that he does not wish to restore family life and
he would not cooperate in the withdrawal of the divorce and custody
proceedings.
8. He states that the 50:50 arrangement contained in the order
dated 25.08.2022 passed by the US Court remains in effect to date
and is not affected by limited legal custody granted to the
applicant by way of order dated 02.12.2022. The Applicant now seems
to take the position that he should not be deprived of certain
benefits conferred upon him under the Order dated 02.12.2022, and
that he should therefore not be required to withdraw it or to
refrain from pressing it. Prima facie, it appears to us that the
applicant does not view the order dated 2nd December, 2022 of the US
Court as a whole and seems to be ignoring various aspects of the
said order and the impact they would have on Respondent No.4 once
she moves to the US. 
9. Be that as it is, today, the applicant has brought around a
situation wherein there is no clarity at present on what the
undertakings he has provided stand for or how they are to be
implemented. 
10. It appears that the parties are engaged in disputes over
various technical aspects of law, and this has caused considerable
confusion as to the next steps to be taken. It is imperative that
what is expected of each party is made abundantly clear. 
11. The best interests of the child require that the Respondent
No.4, who has been her natural guardian for the past four years,
travel with her to the United States, stay there, and take an
active part in her upbringing with equal custody. 

## Page 302

4
12. For the exercise to succeed, three things must be ensured:
1. The Respondent No.4 - Abhilasha, is able to travel
to the United States with her daughter.
2. The Respondent No.4 is able to stay and lead a
comfortable life in the United States, and
3. The Respondent No.4 has equal custody of the child
once she reaches the US.
13. As such, the Respondent No.4 could not have been compelled to
move. 
14. She  has,  however,  agreed  to  do  so.  It  is,  therefore,
imperative  that  her  interests  are  protected  throughout,  as
undertaken by the applicant. 
15. We should not ignore or overlook the fact that, based on the
information provided by the applicant, a case for kidnapping and
child custody deprivation was filed against the Respondent No.4 on
20th October, 2022.
16. A warrant against her is very much active. She is therefore
likely to be arrested as soon as she lands in the United States, in
which event she cannot act as a parent there and the entire
exercise would fail. 
17. The Order dated 25th August, 2022 grants both the parents joint
custody and shared parenting with an equal 50:50 time share on a 4-
3-3-4 schedule, and directs the applicant to pay child support and
temporary spousal support.
18. The Order dated 2nd December, 2022 records the violation of the
Order dated 25th August, 2022 by the Respondent No.4 and directs:
1. The immediate return of the child to the appellant’s
physical custody in California.
2. Sole  custody  to  the  appellant  for  obtaining  and
maintaining the child’s passport.

## Page 303

5
3. Professional supervision of all custody and visitation
of respondent number four. And,
4. Suspension of all spousal and child support until she
complies. 
5. The attorney’s see order as made on August 25, 2022 to
be set aside.
19. While the sole custody is only for passport purposes, the
other directions run against the very arrangement contemplated upon
her return. As the applicant does not wish to withdraw the divorce
and custody proceedings, this Order will continue to operate unless
steps are taken before the US court. 
20. These impediments must be dealt with together with the other
aspects so that all three requirements that we have mentioned above
are met. 
21. We must sufficiently protect the best interests of the child,
which in the present case are intrinsically tied to protecting the
interests of Respondent No. 4. To ensure such protection is
extended, the following questions need to be answered so that there
is complete clarity on what is expected, how the parties propose to
proceed, and what their respective obligations are:
1. What steps will the applicant take, step-by-step, to
have the criminal proceedings against the Respondent
No.4 closed or terminated, the warrant cancelled, and
the closure communicated to the immigration and other
authorities so that she faces no arrest or detention
on arriving in the United States? We say so because
it is the applicant who undertook before this Court
that he would take the necessary steps. 
2. Once the criminal proceedings are closed, what is the
procedure for Respondent No.4 to lawfully enter the
United States, and what steps must she take?
3. What will the applicant do to support that process?
4. How long is the process expected to take, and for how
long will the Respondent No.4 be entitled to stay in
the United States on the visa or status obtained?
5. How and for how long will the applicant support the
Respondent No.4 in the United States, including her
accommodation, finances, and other needs, given that

## Page 304

6
she has no family support there and has to restart
her career?
6. How will the 50:50 shared parenting arrangement work
while the Order dated 2nd December, 2022 remains in
operation,  given  that  it  appears  to  provide
otherwise? What steps will be taken to ensure that
the order dated 25th August, 2022 is followed as it
stands?
7. As the applicant does not wish to withdraw the
proceedings, the custody proceedings before the US
Court will continue. How will it be ensured that the
Order dated 2nd December, 2022, including its finding
that the Respondent No.4 violated the Order dated 25th
August, 2022, does not adversely affect her interests
when the matter is finally decided? We should be
mindful of the statement that was made before us in
the course of the hearing that the applicant does not
intend to take any undue advantage or any benefit of
the Order dated 25th August, 2022 and 2nd December,
2022. 
8. How  will  the  orders  of  this  Court  and  the
arrangements set out above be mirrored before the US
Court and made enforceable there? What steps will the
parties take and by when?
9. Taking all the above together, what is the realistic
timeline for the Respondent No.4 and the child to
travel to the United States? 
22. We are of the firm view that in no circumstances can the child
travel to the United States without her mother. Consequently, the
entire exercise rests on clarity being obtained on each of the
above  aspects,  particularly  the  withdrawal  of  the  criminal
proceedings, the Respondent No.4 obtaining the necessary visa or
status to enter and stay in the United States and Respondent No. 4
having shared custody of the child in the United States without
being prejudiced by the Order dated 02.12.2022, either in the
interim or when the question of custody is finally decided. Until
these aspects are in place, the return of the child cannot be given
effect to in a manner that secures her best interests. 
23. In view of the aforesaid, we keep our final Order dated
8-10-2026 passed in Civil Appeal No.13785/2026 in abeyance. The
applicant shall respond to the questions as stated above in the
form of an affidavit at the earliest. We expect the applicant’s

## Page 305

7
affidavit to be detailed, thorough, and clear on all fronts so as
to ensure there is absolute clarity on the: (i) steps to be taken,
(ii) respective obligations of the parties and (iii) expected
timeframe within which such steps are expected to be taken.
24. It goes without saying that if the applicant takes the
necessary steps as undertaken and recorded by us in our main Order,
it is expected of Abhilasha to extend full cooperation.
25. Notify this matter after four weeks.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.                        of 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No.14461 of 2023)
The District Revenue Officer …. Appellant
Versus
A. Sacractice & Ors. …. Respondents
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Having  comprehensively  looked  at  the  matter  and
considering  the  fact  that  the  issue  of  the  Tamil  Nadu  Land
Encroachment Act, 1905, not being applicable to Grama Natham
lands; which are occupied without even a Patta issued, had come
up before a Full Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in
CA@ SLP (C) No.14461 of 2023                                                                                            Page 1

## Page 313

Kaman  @  Kamatchi  (Died)  Nallasivam  v.  The  District
Collector, Dindigul, District Dindigul and Others in W.P.(MD)
No.19720  of  2017  and  connected  matters,  disposed  of  on
06.03.2026, we are passing this order.  
3. While two Judges of the Full Bench, the majority, found that
mere occupation would suffice, even if the occupant’s name is not
reflected in the Natham Adangal, one of the Judges dissented from
the majority view and found that occupied Natham has not been
clearly  defined  either  under  the  relevant  statute  or  under  the
applicable  legal  framework.  Any  decision  regarding  its  legal
character and vesting cannot be determined conclusively and this
would  only  enable  persons  including  influential  encroachers  to
unlawfully occupy Natham lands and thereafter assert possessory
rights, thereby frustrating the authority of the State and defeating
the object of the governing statutory framework. It was held that
the land shown as Natham or Natham Poramboke in the remarks
column of A-Register or Revenue Settlement Records (RSR), even
if called occupied Natham, always vests with the Government and
CA@ SLP (C) No.14461 of 2023                                                                                            Page 2

## Page 314

consequently the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment
Act,  1905,  can  be  invoked.  The  concurring  and  dissenting
judgments were passed on 06.03.2006.
4. In the context of the above, we are of the opinion that a
comprehensive  hearing  of  the  matter  is  required.  However,
considering the public purpose, we direct the party-respondents to
handover vacant possession of the premises within a period of
three months; within which period, the valuation of the structure
shall  be  carried  out  by  the  Land  Acquisition  Authorities  and
proceedings also taken to fix the compensation for the land and
an  award  passed  in  accordance with  the statutory  framework.
However, the compensation as determined in the award for the
land shall not be disbursed but shall be kept in a Fixed Deposit
Account  bearing  interest.  The  amounts  determined  as
compensation  for  the  structure  shall  be  paid  to  the  party-
respondents within a period of six months. The party-respondents
shall be participated in determining the compensation for both the
building and the land.

7. It is made clear that the learned trial
Court after accepting the provisional bail

bond of the petitioner shall verify the

concealed his antecedent before this Court,
in  that  event,  the  present  provisional
anticipatory  bail  order  shall  not  be
confirmed, but if on verification, it is
found that petitioner is a person with clean
antecedent, in that event, the provisional
anticipatory bail order shall be confirmed
forthwith.
4. Appellant is an accused in Didarganj PS Case No.84
of 2023, registered under Sections 30(a), 36, 32(ii),
(iii) and 41(i)(ii) of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise
Act, 2016.
5. Allegation  against  the  appellant  is  that  1926
litres of liquor were recovered from a vehicle and
another  quantity  of  639.36  litres  of  liquor  were
recovered from a truck. Appellant is the owner of the
said truck.
6. While issuing notice on 10.09.2026, this Court had
passed the following order:
3.  Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner
submits  that  petitioner  had  a  criminal

has certain protections under the Juvenile
