of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short, 'BNS,
2023') and was remanded to police custody vide order
dated 23.10.2025. 
1

## Page 337

3. The appellant filed an application under Section 47
of the Bharatiya Nagarika Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
seeking his release by filing Sessions Case No.49 of
2026 before the Court of Additional Sessions Judge,
Chandigarh. By the order dated 12.03.2026, the said
application  has  been  dismissed.  Thereafter,  the
appellant has filed the impugned Writ Petition,
CRWP-5659-2026,  under  Article  226  of  the
Constitution of India for issuance of a Writ of
Habeas Corpus before the High Court of Punjab and
Haryana at Chandigarh.  Vide  impugned order dated
14.05.2026, the High Court dismissed the said Writ
Petition. Aggrieved by the same, the appellant has
filed the present appeal.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the
parties.
5. On  the  earlier  occasion  i.e.  13.10.2026,  the
following order was passed by this Court.
“Though,  prima  facie,  we  are  not
inclined to agree with the petitioner on
the  issue  of  law  raised,  taking  into
consideration  the  fact  that  the
implication of the petitioner is pursuant
to an extra judicial confession and that
it is a case of circumstantial evidene,
the matter stands adjourned by a period
of two weeks, so as to enable the learned
2

## Page 338

counsel for the respondent - State to
find out the motive form the point of
view of the prosecution.
We make it clear that we will decide
the case on merits on the next date of
hearing.
List the matter on 18.11.2026.”
6. Placing reliance on the material supplied, learned
counsel appearing for the respondent-State submits
that apart from the statement made by the appellant
before the witness in the form of extra judicial
confession, there is a recovery of knife from him.
Reliance has been made on the forensic evidence as
well.
7. Upon hearing the averments made, we find that not
only the fact remains that the appellant has been in
incarceration for more than one year, but also the
stage of the case i.e., the trial having just begun,
is a factor for consideration for granting bail.
Further more, a substantial reliance is made on the
evidence  of  the  witness  before  whom  the  extra
judicial confession is said to have been made by the
appellant. The appellant is not the main accused
even as per the version of the prosecution. The
occurrence, in the present case, took place pursuant
to a brawl after demand was made for payment in an
3

## Page 339

inebriated condition.
8. Taking note of the above, we direct the appellant to
be released on bail, subject to terms and conditions
as may be imposed by the concerned Trial Court.
9. The appeal is allowed, accordingly.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

## Page 343

Singh that he knew Venkat Raman Murti, who could secure
an appointment for Surinder Malik to a Government post.
5. It is further case of the prosecution that Manbir Singh

and  it  was  represented  that  Venkat  Raman  Murti  could
arrange  appointment  of  Surinder  Malik  as  Governor  of
Andaman and Nicobar Islands against a payment of Rs.100
crores and Rs.30 crores is to be paid in advance.

2. A broken marriage has led to the filing of an FIR alleging 
offences under Sections 498A, 294 and 506 read with Section 34 
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Sections 3 and 4 of the 
Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. In the present case, there is an 
additional ground as raised by the appellants herein, the 
father-in-law, mother-in-law and sister-in-law of the 2nd 
respondent; complainant, that the husband; the son of 1st and 
2nd appellants, had filed an application for declaring the 
marriage null and void under Section 12 of the Hindu Marriage 
Act, 1955, which stood dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.  
3. According to the appellants, it was the recalcitrant attitude 
of the 2nd respondent which led to the breakdown of marriage. 
It is alleged that when the 1st appellant’s father died, the 
relatives of the 2nd respondent came to his house and created 
ruckus on 30.11.2021 and again on 06.12.2021. Complaints 

## Page 361

Page 2 of 3 
 
 
were made with respect to the trouble created by the relatives 
of the 2nd respondent which led to the retaliatory FIR filed inter 
alia under Section 498A, is the contention. An application to 
quash the proceedings before the High Court turned futile, 
against which, the appellants have come before this Court. The 
husband, who was a party before the High Court, has not 
challenged the order. 
4. We have gone through the FIR and the statements made by 
the witnesses. The wife, the 2nd respondent, alleged that the 
marriage was solemnized on 09.02.2020 with all pomp and 
ceremony and her family had given a number of household 
articles and a car, in addition to cash. Though for a period, the 
marital life went on smoothly, taunts started regarding the 
insufficiency of dowry. It is also alleged that the marriage 
proposal itself was accepted since the bridegroom was said to 
have a big business in Mumbai. Despite repeated requests, the 
wife was not taken to Mumbai; which the appellants submit, was 
only due to Covid. The fairly long First Information Statement, 
however, makes repeated bland allegations. The statements of 
the wife and the other witnesses, produced as Annexures P6-
P9, also repeat the allegations verbatim, which itself creates a 
suspicion.

5. Admittedly, there was an estrangement of the husband and 
the wife. The allegations made are quite bland and are not 
specific. Despite the allegation of physical assault, there is no 
injury caused, no hospitalization or a medical certificate to 
support the same. 
6. We find absolutely no reason to continue the proceedings 
against the appellants herein who are the father-in-law, mother-
in-law and sister-in-law. We quash the chargesheet produced 
as Annexure P10 pursuant to FIR No.2 of 2022 at the Mahila 
Thana, Gwalior. The proceedings before the Judicial 
Magistrate of the First Class Court, Gwalior, shall stand 
quashed as against the appellants herein. We make it clear that 
we have not made any observations regarding the culpability 
or otherwise of the husband.

       Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
O R D E R
1. An allotment of land has been hanging far from 2003
onwards  despite  Rs.4,96,00,000/-  having  been  paid.
Admittedly,  the  petitioner  herein-Greater  Noida  was
unable to give possession of the plot allotted to the
respondents for building an industrial park. Subsequently
in 2011, a lesser extent of property was offered for the
same valuation which would bring the liability on the
respondent to a little lesser than that originally paid
in 2003; about Rs.3,00,00,000/-. Despite the land having
been allotted in 2011, it is submitted that there were
occupants therein; farmers, who had to be evicted. Vacant
possession is said to have been given in 2018, but the
respondent has objection even to that.
2. In any event, the petitioners made a demand for
amounts by order dated 08.02.2019 and issued a notice
dated 16.08.2021, granting a year’s time to complete the
construction and passed an order dated 10.01.2022; before
the time stipulated, seeking vacant possession of the
2

## Page 372

SLP(C)  No.10162/2026
allotted land; against which order, the revision filed
also stood  dismissed by  order dated  09.05.2023. The
demand dated 08.02.2019 and the orders dated 10.01.2022
and 09.05.2023 were challenged by the respondents herein.
All of which were set aside by the impugned order.
3. We heard Sri Ravindra Kumar, learned Senior Counsel
for the petitioners and Sri Mahesh Jethmalani & Sri Ajay
Kumar Mishra, learned Senior Counsel for the respondents.
4. The High Court on the short ground that though a
notice dated 16.08.2021 had been issued in pursuance of
an amendment made to Section 7 of the Uttar Pradesh
Industrial  Area  Development  Act,  1976,  granting  one
year’s time; prior to expiry of the stipulated period, an
order was passed on 10.01.2022, set aside the same. As a
consequence, the revisional order also stood set aside.
The demand dated 08.02.2019 was also set aside.
5. While the petitioner has very many contentions with
respect  to  the  amounts  due  and  the  laxity  of  the
respondents  in  carrying  out  the  construction,  the
respondents  assert  that  proper  demarcation  was  not
3

## Page 373

SLP(C)  No.10162/2026
carried out and exorbitant amounts have been claimed,
which were not part of the Lease Agreement, without also
granting set off to the excess amounts remaining with the
petitioner. 
6. Insofar as the setting aside of the orders, we find
no reason to interfere with the same because it is not on
merits but on the short ground of the stipulated time in
the notice having not expired. Insofar as the demand is
concerned, we notice that there is no reasoning by the
High Court with regard to the setting aside of the
financial demands made against the respondents. 
7. Though we do not interfere with the impugned order,
we cannot but leave liberty to the petitioner to proceed
in accordance with law, but after giving due opportunity
to the respondents to put forth their contentions; both
against  cancellation  of  lease  as  also  the  monetary
demands made against it. If a notice is issued for
monetary demands, the petitioner should spell out the
specific heads under which such demand is made and give
an opportunity to the respondents to reply to it and
4

## Page 374

SLP(C)  No.10162/2026
afford a personal hearing before any orders are passed.
8. With the above liberty without any observations on
the merits, we dispose of the Special Leave Petition.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

connection with FIR/Crime No. 221 of 2016, registered at
Police Station Sarojini Nagar, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh.
3. The appellant stands convicted by the Trial Court
for the offences punishable under Sections 302, 201, 404,
411 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and has been
sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The criminal
appeal preferred by the appellant against the judgment of
conviction and order of sentence is pending consideration

before the High Court. It is an undisputed fact that the
appellant  has  undergone  nearly  12  years  of  actual
incarceration.

that the case rests entirely on circumstantial evidence and
that, having regard to the heavy pendency of cases before
the High Court, the final hearing of the appeal is likely
to take considerable time.
5. The  prayer for  suspension of  sentence has  been
vehemently opposed by learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-complainant as well as learned counsel appearing
for the respondent-State.
6. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
having regard to the prolonged period of incarceration
already undergone by the appellant, this Court is of the
considered  opinion  that  the  appellant's  prayer  for
suspension of sentence deserves to be allowed.

Court is set aside.

1. IA  No.  245037/2026,  is  an  application  for
deletion of respondent No. 2 from the array of the
parties. The same is allowed at the risk of the
petitioner.
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellant has preferred the present appeal
seeking further enhancement of the compensation awarded
by the High Court.
4. The facts of the case reveal that the appellant
met with an accident on 07.09.2008, as a result of
which  he  sustained  serious  injuries  leading  to
permanent disability.
5. The appellant preferred a claim petition before
1

## Page 381

the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Wayanad, Kalpetta
(hereinafter referred to as the “Tribunal”), which
awarded  compensation  of  Rs.  9,52,100/-  along  with
interest at the rate of 7.5% per annum. In appeal, the
High  Court  enhanced  the  compensation  to  Rs.
23,22,600/-.
6. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant
submits that the appellant was working as a driver and,
on account of the permanent disability sustained in the
accident, has been rendered incapable of pursuing his
profession.  It  is,  therefore,  submitted  that  the
compensation awarded warrants further enhancement.
7. Per contra, learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-Insurance  Company  submits  that  the  High
Court has already enhanced the compensation under the
head of permanent disability from Rs. 4,60,800/- to Rs.
16,12,800/-.
8. This Court has carefully considered the material
available on record and heard learned counsel for the
parties.
9. Having  regard  to  the  peculiar  facts  and
circumstances  of  the  case,  this  Court  is  of  the
considered  opinion  that  a  further  enhancement  of
compensation by a lump-sum amount of Rs. 7,00,000/-
2

## Page 382

(Rupees Seven Lakhs only), towards full and final
settlement of the claim, without any further interest
thereon, would meet the ends of justice.
10. Accordingly, the compensation awarded by the
High  Court  is  further  enhanced  by  a  sum  of  Rs.
7,00,000/- (Rupees Seven Lakhs only). The respondent-
Insurance  Company  is  directed  to  deposit/pay  the
aforesaid enhanced amount to the petitioner within a
period of four weeks from today.
11. The impugned judgment and order passed by the
High Court stand modified to the extent indicated
above. The appeal stands disposed of accordingly.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

the co-accused have been granted the

opinion that no grounds are made out
for  continued  incarceration  of  the
appellant,  Aman  Nathani,  at  this
stage, as the chargesheet has already
been filed. The charges are yet to be
framed.

appeal and direct that the appellant,

bail  in  connection  with  the
aforestated FIR on such appropriate
terms and conditions as may be fixed

course of the trial and shall not take

the  appeal  is  allowed  in  the
aforestated terms.

observations/comments on the merits of
the case and any observation made in

for a period of nine years.

disposal.

and the pendency of the appeal, we are inclined
to set aside the impugned order and grant bail to
the appellant.

aside  and  the  sentence  of  appellant  stands
suspended and he is granted bail on terms and
conditions to the satisfaction of the concerned

to  pay  the  monthly  interest  in  time,  accused  No.  1

his  family  members  and  forcibly  took  custody  of  six
wheeler vehicle for non-payment of the loan amount and
the interest.

No.236/2026 aforestated. Being aggrieved, by the refusal
of the anticipatory bail application by the trial Court and
the High Court respectively, appellant is before this Court.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
@ SLP (CRL.) NO.17786/2026
RANJIT KUMAR MANDAL APPELLANT
                        VERSUS
STATE OF JHARKHAND     RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant, who has been arraigned as an accused in
connection with FIR No.05/2026 registered for the offence
punishable  under  Sections  111(2)(ii),  111(3),  11(4),
317(5), 319(2), 318(4), 338, 336(3), 340(2) 3(5) of the
Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and 66(B), 66(C), 66(D) of
the Information Technology Act, 2000, is seeking for grant
of regular bail.
1

## Page 446

4. It is the case of the prosecution that on receipt of
secret information, the  jurisdictional police  found  three
persons who were hiding in the periphery of the forest
were indulging in committing cyber crime / fraud and on
being apprehended, it was found that they were carrying
several mobile phones, which were used in committing
cyber fraud. Hence, they were arrested.
5. The  jurisdictional  High  Court  in  case  of  Ashish
Mandal who is co-accused has granted regular bail, of
course, having taken note of the fact that there was no
criminal antecedent against him. Though, the learned trial
Judge records in the order rejecting the bail application of
the appellant that there were three complaints against
him, the fact remains that till date there is no FIR which
has been registered against appellant has been placed on
record to establish the antecedents of the appellant.
6. In view of the above, we are of the considered view
that  appellant  is  entitled  for  being  released  on  bail
particularly  in  the  teeth  of  investigation  having  been
completed, chargesheet having been filed and charges
2

## Page 447

also having been framed and as such, he is ordered to be
released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose. Appeal is
allowed accordingly. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
.................J.
  (ARAVIND KUMAR)
.................J.
(VIPUL M. PANCHOLI)
NEW DELHI;
NOVEMBER 18, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.              OF 2026  
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 19371/2026)
PRAMOD      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF RAJASTHAN       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Rajasthan.
3. Appellant was convicted along with another co-accused
under Sections 363, 366A, 384/506 and 376(D)(DA)(2)(n) of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’); Sections 5
and 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences
Act, 2012 (for short, ‘POCSO Act’); and Sections 67A of
the Information Technology Act, 2000. Consequently, the
appellant and the other accused were sentenced to undergo
Rigorous Imprisonment (for short, ‘R.I.’) for 20 years.
4. Aggrieved by the conviction and sentence, appellant
has preferred S.B. Criminal Appeal No.1351 of 2025 before
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at
Jaipur (briefly ‘the High Court’ hereinafter). Along with
the  appeal,  appellant  also  filed  an  application  for
suspension of sentence and for grant of bail, which was
registered as S.B. Criminal Misc Suspension of Sentence
1

## Page 461

Application (Appeal) No.1027 of 2025.
5. By  the  order  dated  08.07.2025,  the  High  Court
dismissed the said application for suspension of sentence.
6. Aggrieved thereby, the related Special Leave Petition
came to be filed before this Court in which notice was
issued on 01.10.2026, pursuant to which respondent-State
of Rajasthan has filed counter affidavit which we have
perused.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant has referred to the
charge-sheet filed by the police before the Court, wherein
it was mentioned that appellant was aged about 17 years 09
months at the time of the incident, which is 22.09.2021;
thus, being a juvenile. However, on orders of the Juvenile
Justice  Board,  appellant  was  tried  as  an  adult  and
convicted as such.
8. Though in the memo of appeal before the High Court,
the ground of juvenility and related issues have not been
urged, considering that the plea of juvenility goes to the
root of the matter and as has been held by this Court that
it can be raised at any point of time, it was rightly
raised before the High Court at the time of hearing of the
miscellaneous application. However, the High Court did not
go into this aspect of the matter and rejected the
suspension application by holding as follows:
“9.The record suggest that appellant Pramod was
released on bail by JJB on 28.06.2022 whereas
Sachin was released on bail in pursuant to
order dated 23.06.2022 in revision petition
2

## Page 462

No.494/2022. Both the appellants were juvenile
on date of incident but the material on record
suggest that a photograph captured by appellant
is circulated to others and moreover money
demanded by Sachin and inability to deliver
money, the appellant Sachin has asked victim to
procure and deliver jewelry from her house.
10. The age of victim is less than 16 years and
it is a heinous offence and looking to entirety
of case, it is not a fit case to enlarge
appellants on bail.”
9. In  the  hearing  today,  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant has placed reliance on a recent decision of this
Court where under somewhat similar circumstances, the
sentence of the appellant was suspended and he was granted
bail during the pendency of the appeal before the High
Court  (Sonu  @  Smart  @  Wasim  Khan  versus  State  of
Rajasthan; Criminal Appeal No.2116 of 2026). He has also
placed reliance on the decision of this Court in Sagar
versus State of Haryana; 2026 INSC 692.
10. While learned counsel for the respondent-State of
Rajasthan would oppose the submissions made on behalf of
the appellant, we feel that this aspect of the matter was
not given due consideration by the High Court. This issue
needs to be addressed.
11. We, accordingly, set aside the impugned order dated
08.07.2025 passed by the High Court and restore S.B.
Criminal Misc Suspension of Sentence Application (Appeal)
No.1027 of 2025 to file.
3

## Page 463

12. We  request  the  High  Court  to  hear  the  matter
(miscellaneous application) afresh and decide the same
within a period of three months from the date of first
mentioning by the parties before the Roster Bench. Since
both the parties are before us, we direct the parties to
appear before the High Court and make a mention on
07.12.2026,  whereafter  we  request  the  High  Court  to
consider the aforesaid application of the appellant in
accordance with law, within the stipulated period.
13. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is disposed of.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 18587 of 2026)
JAYPRAKASH PATIDAR APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
MAGMA H.D.I. GENERAL 
 INSURANCE COMPANY LTD. & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, aged 26 years at the time of
the accident on 21.04.2014, suffered injuries over
his right leg, for which a disability certificate
was issued showing that he has suffered physical
disability of 70%, with 30% improvement expected
with time and vigorous physiotherapy.
3. Indisputably, the appellant was appointed as
Executive – Receivables (VF) in Chola Business
Services Limited, with a monthly basic salary of
Rs.6,500/-  +  House  Rent  Allowance  (HRA)  of
Rs.2,400/-  +  Conveyance  Allowance  of  Rs.700/-,
totaling Rs.9,600/- per month.
4. The Tribunal assessed his monthly income at
Rs.9,600/-  and  taking  the  disability  at  35%,
1

## Page 466

assessed  his  loss  of  income  at  Rs.6,85,440/-
without  calculating  future  prospects.  The  High
Court, therefore, enhanced the amount on this head
by adding 40% towards future prospects, and thus
the total amount of compensation paid by the Motor
Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) at Rs.10,84,520/-
has been enhanced to Rs.14,34,520/-.
5. In this appeal, learned counsel for the
appellant  would  raise  two  main  submissions:
firstly, that his monthly income should have been
taken at Rs.13,515/-, basing the Income Tax Return
for the relevant year, in which his total yearly
income was shown as Rs.1,62,180/-; and secondly,
that the disability should have been taken at 70%
and not 35%.
6. For the first limb of argument, learned
counsel would refer to the judgment rendered by
this Court in the matter of  Anjali & Ors. vs.
Lokendra Rathod & Ors.1 to submit that where Income
Tax Returns are available, the same should be
accepted  to  assess  the  income  of  the
deceased/injured. However, a perusal of the said
judgment would demonstrate that in the said case,
the deceased was a businessman. In the present
case, we are dealing with a claimant who has
1   2022 SCC OnLine SC 1683
2

## Page 467

suffered injuries in an accident and was employed
on a particular monthly salary basis. Thus, where
proof of monthly salary by way of such mention in
the appointment letter is available, a different
figure as income from salary mentioned in the
Income Tax Return, may not be acceptable. It would
have been a different position where the appellant
had  examined  the  employer  to  prove  that,  in
addition to the salary, he was also receiving
incentives  for  which  documentary  proof  is
available, however, such is not the case here.
7. Insofar as, the second argument concerning
disability of 70% is concerned, it is profitable to
refer to the medical certificate, which states that
the  appellant  has  70%  physical  impairment  in
relation to his right leg only, and there is no
certificate that the appellant has suffered 70%
physical impairment of the entire body. Moreover,
the certificate also states that 30% improvement is
expected with time and vigorous physiotherapy.
8. Thus, instead of the disablement worsening
in  due  course,  it  may  improve  with  vigorous
physiotherapy. Therefore, since the injury is only
on one leg, we find that the disability taken at
35% is in accordance with the medical evidence on
record.
3

## Page 468

9. For the foregoing reasons, we do not find
any ground to interfere with the impugned order,
hence the appeal fails and is hereby dismissed.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay in filing the spare copies is condoned.
2. By our order dated 16.10.2026, we had requested the Government
of NCT of Delhi to address itself on the following questions:-
“QUESTIONS TO BE ADDRESSED:- 
I. Which Recruitment Rules govern the vacancy notifications,
such as the one annexed as Annexure P-7 in the petition by Jane
Kaushik, issued by the Delhi Subordinate Services Selection
Board, Government of NCT of Delhi (for short, “DSSSB”)?
a. Whether the said Recruitment Rules are traceable to
any constitutional provision, or statutory enactment, or
State Service Rules. In other words, where does the DSSSB
derive powers to issue the notifications of vacancies in
respect of teaching roles for specific subjects?
II.  Whether  the  aforesaid  Recruitment  rules,  or  statutory
enactment, or State Service Rules require that vacancies in
respect of teaching roles be notified on the basis of gender?
III. If the answer to the above question is in negative, then,
what forms the basis for bifurcation of vacancies between male
and female candidates in a vacancy notification issued by the
DSSSB? In other words, what is the objective behind notifying
vacancies separately for males and females?
IV. If the answer to Q.2 is in affirmative, then, what forms the
basis for using gender as a basis for notifying vacancies in
public recruitment?
V. In both the petitions, do the respondents propose to include
third gender in vacancy notifications issued by them through
DSSSB? In other words, in what manner transgender persons would
be accommodated in public employment?
VI. In the petition by Praveen Singh, insofar as the question of
age relaxation is concerned, why the High Court did not deem it
fit to exercise its power under Rule 12 of the Delhi High Court
2

## Page 472

Establishment (Appointment and Conditions of Service) Rules,
1972,  to  provide  age  relaxation  to  transgender  persons
considering the socio-economic discrimination that they face?”
3. In pursuance of the order passed by this Court, referred to
above, the Directorate of Education, Government of NCT of Delhi has
filed its reply. In para 15 of the reply, the Deponent has stated
as under:-
“15. It is submitted that, henceforth, any advertisement for the
vacancies notified by the Respondent Department shall not be
gender specific. It is further submitted that where any vacancy
notice does specify the requirement of gender as male or female,
the persons in the category of transgender will be entitled to
apply and will be entitled to be considered for being selected
on merits.”
4. Having regard to the specific stance taken by the Government
of NCT of Delhi, as reflected in para 15 of its affidavit referred
to above, substantial issue involved in the matter of Ms. Jane
Kaushik, has been taken care of. 
5. In view of the aforesaid stance, we deem it fit to direct that
the vacancy notices that have already been issued as on the date of
this order and specify the requirement of gender as male or female,
be recalled and re-advertised by the Government of NCT of Delhi
such that the notification of vacancies is not gender specific. The
aforesaid directions shall extend only to such existing vacancy
notices in respect of which the deadline for submitting the
application is not closed yet.   
6. The learned counsel appearing for Ms. Jane Kaushik, the
petitioner in SLP (C) No. 12480/2026 has something to say as

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. By our order dated 16.10.2026, we had requested the Government
of NCT of Delhi to address itself on the following questions:-
“QUESTIONS TO BE ADDRESSED:- 
I. Which Recruitment Rules govern the vacancy notifications,
such as the one annexed as Annexure P-7 in the petition by Jane
Kaushik, issued by the Delhi Subordinate Services Selection
Board, Government of NCT of Delhi (for short, “DSSSB”)?
a. Whether the said Recruitment Rules are traceable to
any constitutional provision, or statutory enactment, or
State Service Rules. In other words, where does the DSSSB
derive powers to issue the notifications of vacancies in
respect of teaching roles for specific subjects?
II.  Whether  the  aforesaid  Recruitment  rules,  or  statutory
enactment, or State Service Rules require that vacancies in
respect of teaching roles be notified on the basis of gender?
III. If the answer to the above question is in negative, then,
what forms the basis for bifurcation of vacancies between male
and female candidates in a vacancy notification issued by the
DSSSB? In other words, what is the objective behind notifying
vacancies separately for males and females?
IV. If the answer to Q.2 is in affirmative, then, what forms the
basis for using gender as a basis for notifying vacancies in
public recruitment?
V. In both the petitions, do the respondents propose to include
third gender in vacancy notifications issued by them through
DSSSB? In other words, in what manner transgender persons would
be accommodated in public employment?
VI. In the petition by Praveen Singh, insofar as the question of
age relaxation is concerned, why the High Court did not deem it
fit to exercise its power under Rule 12 of the Delhi High Court
Establishment (Appointment and Conditions of Service) Rules,
2

## Page 484

1972,  to  provide  age  relaxation  to  transgender  persons
considering the socio-economic discrimination that they face?”
3. In pursuance of the order passed by this Court, referred to
above, the Directorate of Education, Government of NCT of Delhi has
filed its reply. In para 15 of the reply, the Deponent has stated
as under:-
“15. It is submitted that, henceforth, any advertisement for the
vacancies notified by the Respondent Department shall not be
gender specific. It is further submitted that where any vacancy
notice does specify the requirement of gender as male or female,
the persons in the category of transgender will be entitled to
apply and will be entitled to be considered for being selected
on merits.”
4. Having regard to the specific stance taken by the Government
of NCT of Delhi, as reflected in para 15 of its affidavit referred
to above, substantial issue involved in the matter of Ms. Jane
Kaushik, has been taken care of. 
5. In view of the aforesaid stance, we deem it fit to direct that
the vacancy notices that have already been issued as on the date of
this order and specify the requirement of gender as male or female,
be recalled and re-advertised by the Government of NCT of Delhi
such that the notification of vacancies is not gender specific. The
aforesaid directions shall extend only to such existing vacancy
notices in respect of which the deadline for submitting the
application is not closed yet.   
6. The learned counsel appearing for Ms. Jane Kaushik, the
petitioner in SLP (C) No. 12480/2026 has something to say as
regards some relaxation in age, etc. to be provided. In this
3

## Page 485

regard, we shall hear the learned Solicitor General on the next
date of hearing.
7. In the meantime, the Registrar of Delhi High Court shall
submit its response by way of an affidavit within a period of 10
days from the date of this order in respect of Question Nos. V and
VI respectively posed by us in the order dated 16.10.2026. The same
shall be shared with the petitioner for them also to file their
response before the next date of hearing. Insofar as the legal
arguments are concerned, the parties are expected to be prepared on
the next date.
8. List the matters on 10.12.2026.
(HARPREET KAUR)                                 (POOJA SHARMA)

 1. Leave granted.

passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh rejecting the
anticipatory bail prayer of the appellants in connection
with  Crime  No.85/2026  registered  at  Police  Station
Economic Offences Cell, Rewa, District Rewa (M.P.).
4. After  considering  the  submission  of  the  learned
counsel  for  the  appellants,  on  22.08.2026  following
interim order was passed:
“1. The petitioner no.1 had availed
loan  under  a  particular  scheme.
Petitioner  No.2,  husband  of
Petitioner No.1, stood as guarantor.
The  allegations  against  the
petitioners is that they submitted a
false project report and obtained
1

## Page 503

loan for a project which was never
established,  and  the  loan  was
misused and diverted. The contention
on behalf of the petitioners is that
the  entire  loan  amount  has  been
repaid to the Bank and subsidy was
not availed by the petitioners.
2. In such circumstances, according
to  the  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioners,  no  custodial
interrogation is required and the
petitioners are willing to cooperate
in the investigation. Moreover, the
offences with which the petitioners
are  charged  for  in  the  First
Information Report would entail a
punishment not exceeding 07 years.
3. Issue notice, returnable in six
weeks.
4. In the meantime, in the event of
petitioners  arrest  in  connection
with Crime No. 85 of 2026, P.S.
Economic  Offences  Wing  (EOW),
Bhopal, M.P., the petitioners shall
be  released  on  personal  bond  of
Rs.25,000/-  (Rupees  Twenty  Five
thousand  only)  each,  subject  to
undertaking  that  they  shall
cooperate in the investigation and
make  themselves  available  as  and
when investigating agency requires
them  for  interrogation  and  they
shall neither tamper the evidence
nor threaten the witnesses.”
5. Pursuant to service of notice, the State – respondent
is represented.
6. The learned counsel for the respondent - State submits
that the appellants have co-operated in the investigation.
7. Having regard to the nature of the allegations, as
2

## Page 504

also  that  the  appellants  have  co-operated  in  the
investigation,  we  are  of  the  view  that  this  appeal
deserves to be disposed of by making the interim order
absolute subject to the following conditions.
(A) The appellants shall co-operate in the investigation
and make themselves available for interrogation as and
when required by the investigating agency and
(B) Within three weeks from today, they shall submit bail
bonds to the satisfaction of the Trial Court concerned
along with an undertaking that they shall not threaten
the witnesses or tamper the evidence.  
8. The appeal is disposed of in the above terms.

of.

1.  Leave granted.

3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 14.08.2026,
passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at
Chandigarh  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’  hereinafter)
rejecting  the  anticipatory  bail  application  of  the
appellant.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in FIR No.79
of 2026 registered under Sections 61(2), 318(4), 316(2),
319(2), 336(2), 336(3), 338, 340(2) and 351(4) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’) before

## Page 515

the Maqsudan Police Station, District Jalandhar.
5. Allegation against the accused person is of fraud
and forgery of documents for illegal transfer of land.
6. This Court by order dated 24.08.2026 had issued
notice and in the meanwhile granted interim protection
to the appellant subject to the appellant cooperating
with the investigation.
7. Pursuant  to  notice  issued  by  this  Court,
respondent-State of Punjab has filed counter affidavit.
In paragraph 9 of the counter affidavit, it is stated
that petitioner had appeared before the Investigating
Officer (IO) on 07.10.2026 and is cooperating with the
investigation.
8. We further find that appellant is a Civil Engineer
and  is  an  approved  valuer  without  any  criminal
antecedent.  He  was  the  attesting  witness  to  the
agreement to sell which he says he did in good faith.
9. That being the position, we are inclined to make
our order dated 24.08.2026 absolute.
10. Consequently, we set aside the impugned order of
the High Court dated 14.08.2026 and make our order dated
24.08.2026 absolute.

prosecution, as laid in the charge-sheet, is to the effect that Sohail Salim
Qazi (Accused No.1), while being in the company of the present appellant,
had stabbed the deceased/Samir.
4. Though  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  respondent-State,  while
taking  this  Court  to a counter  affidavit filed  as well  as the  additional
documents relatable to the extra-judicial confession, would vehemently
oppose the grant of bail, we are not inclined to accept said contention as
prima facie the role attributed for stabbing the deceased is to the Sohail
1                                                                                      SLP(CRL.) NO.16819 OF 2026

Appellant is ordered to be released on bail.

5.  Having regard to the fact that FIR No. 100/2025 was registered on
21.04.2025 that is after nine days from the date of incident and injury
being simple in nature and also the fact that this Court while issuing
notice had granted an interim protection conditionally by directing the
appellant to appear before the Investigating Officer (IO) and there is no
dispute with regard to appellant having appeared before the IO, we see
no reason as to why the interim order passed earlier should not be made
absolute.

conditions as the jurisdictional IO may deem fit to impose and also on the
condition that appellant would appear before the trial court on all dates of
hearing except when exempted for any specific reason.

1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order  dated
19.06.2026 passed by the Madhya Pradesh High Court
whereby the regular bail prayer of the appellant
has been rejected in connection with FIR/Crime
No.128/2025 registered at P.S. Patan, District
Jabalpur (M.P.).
4. At the outset, the learned counsel for the
appellant  submits  that  he  has  suffered
incarceration for a period exceeding one year six
months and the offences for which the appellant is
being tried are triable by a court of Magistrate.
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.16585/2026 1

## Page 547

5. The learned counsel for the respondent-State
has opposed the prayer for bail
6. Having regard to the fact that offences for
which  the  appellant  has  been  implicated  are
triable by a Court of Magistrate and the appellant
has suffered incarceration for a period exceeding
one year six months, we are of the view that the
appellant is entitled to be released on bail at
this stage.
7. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed.  The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the bail
prayer of the appellant is set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the trial court may
deem fit to impose in the facts and circumstances
of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

BAKSHISH KAUR                                      Appellant(s)

STATE OF PUNJAB                                    Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Punjab & Haryana, by the impugned judgment
and order dated 13.08.2026, has rejected the appellant’s prayer for
bail.
3. The appellant, figuring as an accused in FIR No.69 dated
30.05.2025 registered at Police Station Khuian Sarwar, District
Fazilka under Section 83 of the BNS, was arrested on 3rd March,
2026.
4. The appellant is in jail for the last six months. The
appellant is a 70 years old lady. She is aunt in-law (Bua Sas) and
as per the allegation, she has instigated the deceased to commit
suicide. Learned counsel for the appellant argues before this Court
that the deceased committed suicide in her own matrimonial house
and the present appellant was not at all residing with her. On the
basis of vague and omnibus allegations, she has been roped in. On
the other hand, learned counsel for the State has vehemently
1

## Page 555

opposed the prayer for grant of bail. He has argued before this
Court that the other accused persons are still absconding. 
5. Having regard to the nature of allegations and the period of
incarceration of the appellant, we find that her further detention
in custody is unnecessary; hence, we are inclined to accept the
appeal and grant relief as prayed by admitting the appellant to an
order for grant of bail.
6. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and order.
7. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to furnishing of
bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to
such other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it.
8. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not, directly or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to the court.
9. In the event there is any breach of the terms and conditions
for grant of bail, the trail court shall be at liberty to cancel
the bail of the appellant.
10. It is also ordered that the appellant shall diligently attend
proceedings of the trial, unless exempted. If she is found to
abstain from attending the proceedings without justifiable cause,
that could also be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of
bail and the trial court will be free to pass appropriate orders.
2

## Page 556

11. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant
of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
12. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid terms.
13. Pending applications(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Somnath Dilip Mamdapure                                      ...Appellant

O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The allegation by the 2nd respondent herein is one of sexual assault
as  indicated  in  Annexure  P1-FIR.  The  First  Information  Statement
indicates that the 2nd respondent was married on 11.12.2017 and while
continuing at her marital home, she developed an acquaintance with the
appellant herein who was a bus conductor. It is stated that the appellant
had asked the 2nd respondent to marry him, but the 2nd respondent had
cautioned him that she just merely intended a friendship and nothing
more. It was then alleged that on 09.02.2020, she was forced to go to a
location on the threat levelled by the appellant that he would transmit
the photographs he had on his mobile, to her husband. At the specified
location, the appellant is said to have made sexual overtures outraging
her modesty. 
3. The appellant on the other hand submits that it was a consensual
relationship and he was married in the year 2012 and even before the
relationship commenced with the 2nd respondent, she too had married

## Page 559

2
and had a son in the wedlock. It is also pointed out that a subsequent
FIR lodged by the 2nd respondent on graver allegations was quashed. It
was alleged that on 13.01.2025, after the first FIR was lodged in 2020,
the appellant had again visited the complainant’s sister’s house and had
physical relations with her under the promise of marriage. 
4. The subsequent criminal case stood quashed by the High Court of
Judicature at Bombay Bench at Aurangabad by Annexure P11. It was
categorically found therein that the statements of witnesses, which were
part of the chargesheet, clearly indicate that the prosecutrix who is an
independent adult had voluntarily entered into a romantic relationship
after exercise of free and conscious choice, fully knowing the marital
status of the appellant and herself. There was no reason to accept the
version of the prosecutrix that she entered into the relationship on the
promise of marriage.
5. We also notice the WhatsApp messages produced as Annexure P3,
which  indicate  consensual  relationship  and  there  was  a  notarized
undertaking  executed  by  the  appellant  and  the  2nd respondent  on
13.05.2025, produced as Annexure P4, wherein they agreed to end their
consensual relationship.
6. The instant FIR which is sought to be quashed was far earlier in time;
year 2020. Therein no allegation of physical relationship was stated. The

## Page 560

3
allegation then was that though appellant had forced her to marry him,
she refused and then the appellant threatened her with photographs and
attempted  to  outrage  her  modesty.  Obviously,  the  relationship
commenced in the year 2020 and continued even in the year 2025. The
latter FIR, which stood quashed, was also on the ground that there was a
physical relationship established. 
7. We find absolutely no reason to sustain the order impugned and set it
aside.  We also  notice that the 2nd respondent,  who was issued  with
notice, has not appeared before us. We find that this is a clear case of
abuse of process of law and we quash the chargesheet filed as RCC
No.384  of  2020  before  the  Judicial  First  Class  Magistrate’s  Court,
Osmanabad, produced as Annexure P2 and direct that no further steps
be taken in the said proceedings.
8. The appeal is allowed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

High Court, however, reduced the sentence visited upon the
appellants from imprisonment for three years to imprisonment
for nine months.

sentence of imprisonment imposed upon both the appellants, we
deem it appropriate to reduce the sentence further to a period

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  applications  bearing  I.A.  Nos.
341984/2026, 341988/2026 and 341993/2026 seeking
substitution  to  bring  on  record  the  legal
representatives of the deceased respondent ‘Dr. N.
Paevathaiah’,  setting  aside  abatement  and
condonation  of  delay  in  filing  the  same  are
allowed.

## Page 626

2
2. Accordingly,  delay  stands  condoned  and
abatement, if any, is set aside.
3. The cause title be amended accordingly.
4. We have heard Advocates M. Vijaya Bhaskar
and K. V. Girish Choudhary, appearing for the
Judgment  Debtor(‘JDR’)  and  Decree  Holder(‘DHR’)
respectively.
5. The petitioner challenges the order dated
15.10.2026 through which the High Court has ordered
notice to the legal representatives of the deceased
sole respondent.
6. It has been brought to our notice that the
Execution Petition is at a very advanced stage and
sale proclamation was also taken forward. However,
the sale could not be completed on account of a few
omissions noted in the process of conducting the
sale. The DHR objects to considering passing any
order by this Court.
7. We  take  note  of  the  fact  that  the
application has been filed to bring the legal
representatives of the deceased sole respondent on
record. We cannot also find fault with the order of
the High Court for the simple reason that as long
as the array of parties is not effective, no order
can be passed. While considering the prayer in I.A.
No. 1 of 2022, we grant stay of the impugned decree

## Page 627

3
and judgment in O.S. No. 16 of 2013 subject to the
petitioner depositing the decreetal amount and cost
within four weeks from today.
8. The special leave petition stands disposed
of in the above terms.
9. There shall be stay of O.S. No. 16 of 2013
till the disposal of A.S. No. 587 of 2019.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

O R D E R
1.  Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. Appellant  was  convicted  by  the  Mahila  Court,
Cuddalore, Tamil Nadu in Special Sessions Case No.46 of
2018 under Section 366 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(for short, ‘IPC’) and under Section 6 of the Protection
of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012.
Accordingly,  he  was  sentenced  to  undergo  Rigorous
Imprisonment (RI) for a term of 5 years and to pay fine
of 5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand Only) with a default₹
stipulation for the offence under Section 366 IPC and to
undergo RI for 14 years and to pay fine of 10,000/-₹
(Rupees Ten Thousand Only) with a default stipulation
1

## Page 644

for the offence under Section 6 of the POCSO Act; both
the sentences to run concurrently.
4. Aggrieved by the conviction and sentence, appellant
preferred appeal before the High Court of Judicature at
Madras (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter) which was
registered as Criminal Appeal No.253 of 2019.
5. By the judgment and order dated 26.02.2021, the
High Court dismissed the Criminal Appeal and affirmed
the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant.
6. We find that out of 14 years of RI, appellant has
undergone 8 years of incarceration without remission.
7. In the circumstances, we are inclined to suspend
the sentence and grant bail to the appellant.
8. Consequently, the sentence imposed on the appellant
is suspended and he is directed to be released on bail
on usual terms and conditions.
9. List the Criminal Appeal for hearing in due course.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner had instituted proceedings before
the Waqf Tribunal claiming himself to be Mutawalli of
Dargah Hazrat Khalifat-UR Raheman Rehmat-Ulla-Alia as
also  its  Sajjadanashin.  Admittedly,  the  term  of
1

## Page 650

Mutawalli, as appointed by the Board, has lapsed. As
a consequence, the other side raised a plea that
petitioner cannot pursue the proceedings.
2. The proceedings are in the name of Waqf and not
in the personal capacity of either the Sajjadanashin
or  the  person  interested  in  the  Waqf.  In  such
circumstances, the question which arises for our
consideration is whether those proceedings can be
continued by the Mutawalli whose term has expired.
3. The contention on behalf of the petitioner is
that since the petitioner has set up a plea that he
is also Sajjadanashin of the Waqf concerned, and
Sajjadanashin has no specified term, he has a right
to represent the Waqf and, therefore, continue the
proceedings.
4. What is relevant to be considered is whether in
absence of any Waqfnama or a Waqf deed, and in
absence  of  any  custom  pleaded  in  the
plaint/application preferred before the Tribunal by
the petitioner of him being the Sajjadanashin of the
Dargah concerned, having accepted his appointment as
a Mutawalli, could he continue to represent the
Waqf/Dargah on expiry of his term as the Mutawalli.
5. The learned counsel for the petitioner prays for
2

## Page 651

time to study the matter and assist the court on the
above aspect.
6. List on 25.11.2026.

Ministry of Home Affairs with the participation of certain
high dignitaries in the month of December, 2026. Besides the
issues which are the subject matters of the present Original

consider granting some time.

expressed the same, views as expressed by the learned Attorney

Therefore, the issues are not so complicated, and the matter
stands pending for quite some time. Learned Senior counsel
also make reference to the earlier order(s) passed by this
Court clearly indicate that the present matter would be heard
up at the earliest.

7. In the meantime, we expect the parties to arrive at a

For Respondent(s) 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  respondent No.1 has preferred a Writ Petition
challenging the notice dated 20.09.2025 issued by the
petitioner, informing him that he will attain the age of
superannuation on 30.06.2026.
2. Since, according to the respondent No.1, this notice
was issued basing on his incorrect date of birth in the
service record, he preferred a Writ Petition seeking change
1

## Page 704

in date of birth, and subsequently, he moved an interim
application seeking stay of the notice of superannuation.
3. Learned Single Judge of the High Court,  vide its
order dated 02.07.2026, stayed the superannuation notice,
against which, the petitioner preferred a Writ Appeal, and
the Division Bench, under the impugned order, has modified
the order to the extent that the petitioner shall have the
right to restitution of the amount that may be paid to the
respondent No.1 as a consequence of the Single Judge's
order, in the event they succeed in the litigation.
4. When this Special Leave Petition came up for hearing
on 02.09.2026, this Court had stayed the order passed by
the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench, under
which the notice of superannuation was stayed.
5. However, it is to be seen that during the pendency
of the Writ Petition, the respondent No.1 has already
attained the age of superannuation as on 30.06.2026.
6. In view of the above, we dispose of the Special
Leave Petition directing that the Writ Petition preferred
by the respondent No.1 be decided on its own merits, and if
any Contempt Petition has been preferred by the respondent
No.2 alleging violation of the Single Judge's order dated
02.07.2026, the same shall remain stayed till the Writ
Petition is decided by the learned Single Judge of the High
Court.
2

of.

Etc.1,  we do not find any error in the direction

from the date on which his juniors were promoted
provided he is found fit and eligible as per the
report.

with the directions [(i),(ii),(iii),(iv) and (v)] in
paragraph 42 of the impugned order.

that there are certain findings in the impugned order

possible to save the marriage. Although the wife wants to

ways honorably and peacefully.

will pay a lump sum amount of Rs.12,00,000/- (Rupees Twelve
Lakh only) to his wife as full and final settlement and will
continue to pay Rs.10,000/- (Rupees Ten Thousand only) per
month towards maintenance of his minor daughter till the
daughter attains the age of 21. If this proposal is accepted
by the wife, we shall proceed further to pass appropriate
order. If its not acceptable, then it is for the wife to
decide the future course of action.

seeking grant of  bail. The petition is, accordingly,
dismissed.  However, considering the fact that five

of six months.

petitioner is highly deprecated. At this juncture, the learned Senior Counsel
seeks  leave  of the  Court to withdraw the said averment made in the SLP.

by  3079  days.  No  justifiable  cause  was  shown  in  the
application seeking condonation of delay filed along with the
second appeal. 
In this background, we are of the opinion that the High
Court was justified in dismissing the second appeal on the
ground of delay. 
The special leave petition lacks merit and is dismissed
as such. 
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
(SACHIN)                                     (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioners
and  learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh.
2. In  all  the  03  Special  Leave  Petitions,
petitioners have made a categorical statement that
they do not have any criminal antecedent. However, in
the  counter-affidavits  filed  on  behalf  of  the
respondent-State of Chhattisgarh, it is pointed out
that there are criminal antecedents as against each
of the petitioners.
3. Though  petitioners  have  filed  rejoinder
affidavits, there is no averment as to why there was
an omission to mention about the criminal antecedents
of  the  petitioners.  In  the  hearing  also,  no
explanation is forthcoming.
4. In the circumstances, we decline to extend the
benefit of bail to the petitioners.
5. Petitioners  may  renew  their  prayer  for  bail
before the appropriate forum.
6. Subject to the above, the Special Leave Petitions
are dismissed.
7. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
(ABHINAV KUMAR)                                (CHETNA BALOONI)

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Ranjan Mukherjee- 1042, AOR
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the petitioners -
convicts.
3. We are of the view that no error, not to speak of any error
of law, could be said to have been committed by the High Court
in  passing  the  impugned  Judgment  and  Order  holding  the
petitioners guilty of the alleged offence of murder.
4. However, we take notice of the fact that the petitioners -
convicts are undergoing sentence past more than 12 years and 06
months.
5. In such circumstances, we permit the petitioners to prefer an
appropriate representation, addressed to the competent authority
of the State Government praying for remission of sentence.
6. If any such representation is preferred by the petitioners,

## Page 1083

2
the competent authority shall look into the same expeditiously
and take appropriate decision on the same, having regard to the
Remission Policy of the State Government prevailing on the date
of the commission of the alleged crime or any other remission
policy  that  may  be  more  beneficial  to  the  petitioners  -
convicts.
7.  With  the  aforesaid,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  stands
disposed of.
8. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

service through speed post for which service was duly affected.
From the above, it is clear that the respondent is not
responding  to  the  communications  itself  and,  therefore,  not
inclined to comply with the direction issued by this Court. 

## Page 1113

2
In such view of the matter, we have no other option
except to issue bailable warrants against the respondent to secure
his presence before this Court, along with the Child, on the next
date of hearing, failing which non-bailable warrants shall be
issued. 
Accordingly, bailable warrants, in the sum of Rs.50,000/-
(Rupees Fifty Thousand), with one surety of the like amount, be
issued against the respondent, to secure his presence in this Court
on 09.12.2026. The concerned Police shall ensure the service of the
bailable warrants on the respondent.
List on 09.12.2026.
(SWETA BALODI)                                  (POONAM VAID)

CORAM :

         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE SUNITA AGARWAL
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Siddharth Jain- 2811, AOR
Mr. Souumyajit Pani, Adv.
Mr. Varun, Adv.
                   
For Respondent(s) :  
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel for the petitioners.
2. We are not inclined to interfere with the impugned
judgment and order passed by the High Court. Rather, we find
it astonishing that the petitioner(s) proceeded to file the
present Special Leave Petition.
3. It is apparent from the facts that the father of the
respondent was appointed on 05.07.1991 against an oustee
quota.  He was regularized and thereafter unfortunately died
in harness on 25.11.2013 after rendering more than 21 years
1

## Page 1169

of  service.   During  his  service  no  one  had
challenged/questioned his eligibility for appointment as an
oustee.  It is on the claim being made for appointment by
the respondent as a dependent on him i.e. son that the
questions are being raised.  The High Court has dealt with
this aspect in detail and has rightly come to the conclusion
with  regard  to  the  entitlement  of  appointment  of  the
respondent.  Questioning this aspect itself indicates non-
application of mind.
4. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, dismissed
with costs of 1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh only), to be paid₹
to the respondent within three (3) weeks from today.
5. A report regarding compliance/payment of cost shall be
filed in the Registry within five (5) weeks from today.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned. 
2. The petitioner has been denied anticipatory bail by the High
Court in connection with FIR No.5114033250266 of 2025 registered at
PS Maniyari, District Muzaffarpur under Section 80 read with 3(5)
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
3. The case concerns an alleged dowry death, wherein the deceased

## Page 1213

2
was found hanging. The Petitioner, being the brother of the
deceased's  father-in-law,  is  alleged  to  have  threatened  the
deceased with death.
4. High  Court  rejected  the  Petitioner’s  anticipatory  bail
application on the ground that there is specific allegation against
the Petitioner supported by witnesses.
5. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that the co-
accused, being father-in-law and mother-in-law of the deceased were
granted anticipatory bail by a Co-ordinate Bench of the High Court,
and that the Petitioner lived separately from the deceased and her
husband and has no concern with her in-law’s family. 
6. Having  heard  the  learned  counsel  for  the  parties,  and
considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the
opinion that the material against the petitioner falls short of the
threshold required for refusal of anticipatory bail. 
7. Therefore, we order that in the event of arrest of the
petitioner in connection with the offence enumerated above, he
shall be released on bail, subject to terms and conditions that the
Investigating Officer may deem fit to impose. He is also required
to cooperate in the investigation. 
8. Once the petitioner is released on bail by the IO, on
directions issued by the IO or summons issued by the jurisdictional
Court, the petitioner shall appear before the jurisdictional Court
and furnish fresh bail bonds and ensure due appearance in the
trial.
9. With the aforesaid, this petition stands disposed of.
10. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Exemption Applications are allowed.
2. The petitioner has been convicted under Section 302 IPC and
was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life and was imposed a
fine of Rs. 2,000/- (Rupees two thousand) with default imprisonment
of three months of rigorous imprisonment by the Trial Court in
connection with FIR No.150/2020 registered at PS Shujalpur City,

## Page 1215

2
District Shajapur, Madhya Pradesh. The Petitioner has preferred an
appeal against the order of conviction before the High Court; and
is seeking suspension of his sentence, pending appeal before the
High Court. The Petitioner has undergone over six years and five
months in judicial custody since 09.06.2020.
3. The petitioner is alleged to have committed the murder of his
daughter-in-law by pouring kerosene oil and setting her ablaze. The
allegation is founded on the dying declaration of the deceased. The
High Court vide the impugned order denied suspension of sentence
considering  the  nature  of  allegations  levelled  against  the
Petitioner.
4. The learned Counsel for the Petitioner submitted that there is
no eyewitness to the occurrence to implicate the petitioner in the
alleged specific act of setting the deceased on fire. It was
further submitted that the deceased was not mentally stable and
suffered from schizophrenia and depression for which she was being
treated by DW-3 who stated that she had not returned for treatment
since January 2020.
5. On a prima facie consideration, especially the period of
incarceration, we suspend the sentence of the petitioner pending
appeal.
6. The  Petitioner shall be released on bail on such conditions
as the trial court may deem fit to impose, till the disposal of the
appeal before the High Court.
7. With the aforesaid, this Special Leave Petition is disposed
of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
